A role that includes your keychain grants its keys to every user who holds that role, in every organization.

{{< alert title="Note" >}}

If you do not hold View Keychains in the selected organization, the Keychains tab shows a permission error. Every default user role holds View Keychains through User View. Create Keychain stays disabled until you use a Provider Admin account.

{{< /alert >}}

#### View Keychains

Review keychains by navigating to the [Keychains](https://cloud.layer5.io/security/keychains) page. Anyone holding View Keychains can open the tab. The list shows system-owned keychains and the viewer's own.

{{< alert title="Note" >}}

If you do not hold View Keychains for your selected organization, you will see a disabled Keychains tab. Switch to an organization where your role includes View Keychains, or ask an Organization Admin to check your role.

{{< /alert >}}

#### Assign Keychains

Including a keychain in a role, or removing it, is a Provider Admin action. The server requires the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. Organization Admin does not hold Assign Keychains to Roles.

1. Open the [Roles](https://cloud.layer5.io/security/roles) page as a Provider Admin.
2. Add the keychain to a role, or remove it. See [Roles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/roles/_index.md" >}}). The change applies to that role in every organization, because roles are global.
3. Assign the role to the users who need it, in the organization where they need it. See [Users]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/_index.md" >}}).

Test with a user who holds the role. Sign in as that user in a specific organization and confirm the controls the keys govern are enabled.

{{< alert title="Permission Assignment at Teams, Organization and Provider Levels" >}}

1. Team Admin can assign roles to users in a team. Team Admin cannot create, edit, or assign keychains.
2. Organization Admin can assign roles to users in an organization. Organization Admin cannot create, edit, or assign keychains.
3. Only Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete a keychain, add or remove its keys, or include it in a role. The server checks that role across the whole deployment.

{{< /alert >}}

### Keychains Lifecycle

Layer5 Cloud ships with 30 default keychains. The system account owns them. Only a Provider Admin can add or remove keys on a default keychain, or on any other keychain.

- **Deleting a keychain** removes its key mappings, so the keychain stops granting anything immediately, in every role that included it. Deleting is a soft delete.
- **Removing a key from a keychain** stops that key flowing to every role that includes the keychain.
- **Adding a key to a keychain** grants it to every holder of every role that includes the keychain.

Authorization is evaluated on every request, so users gain or lose access on their next action, without signing in again.

{{< alert title="Best Practice" >}}

Default roles carry the default keychains, and every new user receives a default role. A change to a default keychain therefore changes permissions for users across the deployment, regardless of organization. Leave default keychains as shipped unless that is the intended outcome.

On a self-hosted deployment, to grant a different combination of keys, a Provider Admin creates a new keychain and includes it in a new role, and then the role is assigned to the users who need it. Keychains and roles are shared by every organization, so per-organization differences come from which roles a user holds in that organization.

{{< /alert >}}

### Who can change a keychain

Keychains and their assignment to roles apply across the whole provider, not to one organization. Only a Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete a keychain, add or remove its keys, or include it in a role or remove it from one. This is the rule as of Layer5 Cloud v1.0.280.

Layer5 Cloud enforces keychain operations in two places. The interface enables or disables each control based on the keys you hold. The server checks the matching key and then confirms that the caller holds the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. Holding the Provider Admin role inside one organization does not satisfy that check.

| Operation | Who can do it | Where it is enforced |
|---|---|---|
| View the keychain list and a keychain's keys | Anyone holding View Keychains, which every default user role holds through User View. The list shows system-owned keychains and the viewer's own. | Interface: the Keychains tab requires View Keychains. Server: returns only system-owned keychains and the caller's own. |
| Create a keychain | Provider Admin. The interface also requires Create Keychain. | Server and interface |
| Rename a keychain, add keys, remove keys | Provider Admin. The interface also requires Edit Keychain. | Server and interface |
| Delete a keychain | Provider Admin. The interface also requires Delete Keychain. | Server and interface |
| Include a keychain in a role, or remove it | Provider Admin | Server |

When the server refuses a change to a keychain, it answers HTTP 403 with a JSON error. A caller who lacks the route's key receives code `meshery_cloud-1108`. A caller who holds the key without being a Provider Admin for the whole deployment receives code `meshery_cloud-3336`, "Only a Provider Admin can change roles, keychains or permission keys".

{{< alert title="Note" >}}
Create Keychain, Edit Keychain, Delete Keychain, and Assign Keychains to Roles belong to the Provider Management keychain, so by default only Provider Admins see these controls enabled. Everyone else can still view keychains.
{{< /alert >}}

### Change the keys in a keychain

**Needs:** the Provider Admin role. The interface also requires Edit Keychain.

Open the keychain's update dialog, rename it, or change the selected keys. The interface adds and removes only the difference. Removing a key stops that key flowing to every role that includes the keychain, immediately.

### Delete a keychain

**Needs:** the Provider Admin role. The interface also requires Delete Keychain.

Delete the keychain from its row and confirm in the "Delete Keychain" dialog. Deleting removes the keychain's key mappings. The keychain stops granting anything at once, for every role that included it.

As with every keychain, only a Provider Admin can edit or delete a default keychain.

### Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The Keychains tab shows a permission error | You lack View Keychains in the selected organization. | Ask an Organization Admin to check your role. |
| Create Keychain is disabled | You lack the Create Keychain key. | Use a Provider Admin account. |
| `403` with code `meshery_cloud-1108` or `meshery_cloud-3336` | You are not a Provider Admin for the whole deployment. Keychains and their assignment to roles apply across the whole provider. | Ask a Provider Admin to make the change. |
| A user still lacks a capability | The keychain is not on the user's role, or the user holds the role in a different organization. | Add the keychain to the role, and check the role is held in the organization in use. |

### Keychain endpoints

Success responses are JSON unless stated. Errors from these handlers return a plain-text message. Refusals from the authorization layer return JSON. Paths sit under `/api`. Owning a keychain does not authorize a change to it. For a Provider Admin, a malformed keychain id on these routes returns `400` with a plain-text message.

| Method and path | Who may call | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /auth/keychains` | Signed-in user | Lists keychains you can see. Parameters: `page`, `pageSize`, `order`, `search` (matches the keychain name). |
| `GET /auth/keychains/{keychainId}` | Signed-in user | Returns one keychain. |
| `GET /auth/keychains/{keychainId}/keys` | Signed-in user | Lists the keys in a keychain. `search` matches the key description. |
| `POST /auth/keychains` | Provider Admin holding Create Keychain | Creates a keychain owned by the caller. Only the `name` in the body is used. |
| `PUT /auth/keychains/{keychainId}` | Provider Admin holding Edit Keychain | Updates the keychain name. |
| `POST /auth/keychains/{keychainId}/{keyId}` | Provider Admin holding Edit Keychain | Adds a key. |
| `DELETE /auth/keychains/{keychainId}/{keyId}` | Provider Admin holding Edit Keychain | Removes a key. |
| `DELETE /auth/keychains/{keychainId}` | Provider Admin holding Delete Keychain | Soft-deletes the keychain and its key mappings. |
| `POST` and `DELETE /identity/orgs/{orgId}/roles/{roleId}/keychains/{keychainId}` | Provider Admin holding Assign Keychains to Roles | Adds or removes a keychain on a role. Roles are global, so the change applies in every organization. |

See [Keys]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keys.md" >}}) for the individual permissions, and [Cloud API]({{< ref "cloud/reference/api-reference/_index.md" >}}) for authentication and the organization header.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Platform Development Guide"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/academy/platform-development/index.md
description: An advanced guide to the Layer5 Academy architecture, multi-repository workflow, and development best practices for contributors.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This guide walks you through the Layer5 Academy platform's multi-repository architecture. You will learn the role of each core component and master the practical workflows for theme development, local testing, and end-to-end validation with Layer5 Cloud.

## The Multi-Repository Model

The [Layer5 Academy platform](https://cloud.layer5.io/academy) is built on a "separation of concerns" architecture. Instead of a single monolithic repository, we use a multi-repository model where content, style, and build configurations are managed independently. This approach keeps the system modular, simplifies maintenance, and allows teams to work on different parts of the platform concurrently.

At a high level, the `academy-theme` provides the visual style for content from repositories like `academy-example`, and the `academy-build` repository acts as the central factory, assembling everything into the final website.

## Core Repositories

The Layer5 Academy platform is composed of several core repositories.

### [academy-theme](https://github.com/layer5io/academy-theme)

This repository is the "skin" for the entire Academy. It controls the website's design, including all the layouts, colors, and fonts.

Content repositories automatically import this theme as a Go Module. As a content creator, you do not need to fork or clone this repository; your academy will use these styles by default. 

> Currently, we only support customizing shortcodes in your content repository, not full theme customization. For requests regarding new archetypes, layouts, or theme enhancements, please open an issue in the [academy-theme repository](https://github.com/layer5io/academy-theme/issues).

### [academy-example](https://github.com/layer5io/academy-example)

This is the "starter kit" for anyone new to creating Academy content. It provides a pre-configured site that new organizations can fork to get started quickly.

> [Learn How]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/creating-your-learning-path/index.md" >}}) to create your own learning path

This content repository doesn't build the final website itself. Instead, it uses an automated workflow to act as a "gatekeeper" for new content. When you create a new GitHub Release, it triggers the following process:

1. **Sanity Check**: It first runs a local build to ensure the new content has no fundamental errors that would break the site.

2. **Publishing Notification**: If the check passes, it calls a reusable action from the `academy-build` repository. This action securely sends a request to the Layer5 Cloud API, using your configured `ACADEMY_ORG_ID` and `ACADEMY_TOKEN` secrets.

{{< alert type="info" title="Publishing Trigger" >}}
This request effectively says: "A new version of content is ready for this organization. Please update it." This workflow does not build the final site; it only validates the content and notifies the build system.
{{< /alert >}}

### [academy-build](https://github.com/layer5io/academy-build)

**This is the central hub of the entire system.** It contains the main Hugo configuration for the production build and uses Go Modules to manage the versions of all content modules and the `academy-theme`.

When its workflow is triggered, an automated process acts like a master assembly line:

1.  **Collects Parts**: It begins by gathering all the necessary components—`academy-theme` and all the course content from the various content repositories.

2.  **Assembles the Website**: Next, it combines everything. It applies the theme's design to all the course content, building a single, complete website.

3.  **Deploys Online**: Finally, it takes the newly built website and automatically pushes it to the cloud platform, making the updates live for everyone to see.

If the build fails, the previous version of your Academy stays live. The content repository's own workflow validates and notifies. It does not build the site learners see. Publishing a release is accepted only from an organization admin or owner.

## Developer Workflows

### How to Develop and Preview Locally

Use this workflow for rapid local development and iteration. If you're only changing Markdown files and want a fast preview loop, run these commands within a content repository (such as `layer5-academy`):

{{< alert type="info" title="layer5-academy as an Example" >}}
We'll use [layer5-academy](https://github.com/layer5io/layer5-academy) for these examples because it hosts all official Layer5 learning paths. It serves as a feature-complete reference, allowing you to see how a complex, real-world content repository is structured.
{{< /alert >}}

1. `go mod tidy`: Cleans up and verifies Go module dependencies.
2. `make setup`: Installs necessary tools and modules.
3. `make site`: Starts the local Hugo development server.

You can then view your content by navigating to `http://localhost:1313/academy`.

Local preview shows structure, content, and links. It does not show your organization's branding, and it cannot score assessments, count attempts, or record progress, because those run on the Layer5 Cloud server.

### How to Develop the Academy Theme

If you need to modify the `academy-theme` and see its effect on real content, you'll use the `go mod replace` directive:

1. **Modify the Theme**: Make your code changes in your local clone of the `academy-theme` repository.
2. **Redirect the Dependency**: In the `go.mod` file of the content repository you're using for previewing (e.g., `layer5-academy`), add a `replace` directive to point Hugo to your local theme directory:
   ```go
   replace github.com/layer5io/academy-theme => ../academy-theme
   ```
3. **Apply Changes and Relaunch**: Run `go mod tidy` to apply the `replace` directive you just added. Then, restart the server with `make site`. The local server will now use your local theme code, allowing you to see your changes instantly.

### How to Use End-to-End Testing with Layer5 Cloud

Use this workflow for end-to-end testing that mirrors the production environment. This is the ultimate way to verify your changes work correctly within the Layer5 Cloud UI before they go live:

All steps in this section should be performed from the root of your local `academy-build` repository.

1.  **Install Dependencies**: Run this command once to install necessary dependencies.
    ```bash
    make setup
    ```

2. **Prepare Local Dependencies**: If you're testing local changes from other repositories (like a theme or content module), edit the `go.mod` file in `academy-build` to point to your local versions using a replace directive:
   ```go
   replace github.com/layer5io/academy-theme => ../academy-theme
   replace github.com/layer5io/layer5-academy => ../layer5-academy
   ```

3.  **Build for Staging**: Run the command to build the entire Academy site specifically for the staging environment.
    ```bash
    make stg-build
    ```

4.  **Sync with Cloud**: After the build completes, run the following command to sync the generated static files with the Layer5 Cloud staging environment:
    ```bash
    make sync-with-cloud
    ```

5. **Preview on Staging**: Your changes will be available on the [staging environment](https://staging-cloud.layer5.io/) within approximately 10 minutes.

{{< alert type="warning" title="Local vs. Cloud Discrepancies" >}}
The local preview (`make site`) is excellent for rapid development, but it is **not** a 100% accurate representation of the final product. The Cloud UI acts as a wrapper around the Academy content, which can introduce subtle differences. These are often caused by CSS class conflicts or variations in JavaScript execution within the larger application.

**Always verify your changes in the staging environment before considering them complete.**
{{< /alert >}}

### When to Use a Holistic Build Test

If you need a faster way to check the final output without syncing to the cloud, you can run a production-like build locally from the `academy-build` repo:

```bash
make prod-build
```

This command generates the final static files in the `public/` directory. You can inspect the generated HTML and JSON files here to diagnose build-time issues before deploying.

### Best Practices

1. **Keep Dependencies Clean**: After testing with local replace directives in your `go.mod` file, always remember to remove them and run `go mod tidy` before committing your changes. This prevents accidental check-ins of local paths.
2. **Test Incrementally**: Start with local development for rapid iteration, then progress to holistic builds, and finally test in the staging environment.
3. **Version Control**: Always commit your changes to version control before testing in staging to ensure you can track and revert changes if needed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Account Consolidation"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/account-consolidation/index.md
description: Layer5 Cloud resolves email/password, GitHub sign-in, and Google sign-in to a single account per verified email address.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Account consolidation merges every duplicate Layer5 Cloud account that belongs to one person into a single canonical account. The canonical account takes ownership of the duplicates' designs, connections, memberships, roles, and other data, keeps their email addresses so old sign-ins still land in the right place, and retires the duplicates.

{{< alert type="info" title="Operator-only" >}}
Consolidation is a command-line tool, `consolidate-users`, that a deployment operator runs with direct database access. It is not an API, not a UI feature, and not automatic. Customers of the Layer5-hosted service cannot trigger it and have no control over it. Operators of a self-hosted Layer5 Cloud run it themselves.
{{< /alert >}}

## What changed

The identity provider behind Layer5 Cloud could create a separate account for each sign-in method one person used. A person who registered with a password and later signed in with GitHub or Google could end up with two or three accounts, even when they shared the same email address. Designs, organizations, and workspaces created under one sign-in method appeared to disappear when the person signed in with another.

Consolidation treats each group of accounts that belong to one person as a cluster and collapses the cluster into one account. For each affected person, resources move to a single retained account, including:

- Designs and views
- Workspaces and environments
- Connections and credentials
- Performance profiles and results
- Schedules
- API tokens
- Organization and team memberships and roles
- Keychains and keys
- Teams the duplicate owns
- Invitations the duplicate created
- Academy registrations and test submissions
- Event trackers
- Resource access grants

Revoked tokens stay on the retired account on purpose and still read as revoked.

Organizations are handled separately from that transfer. An organization owned by a duplicate account with no other active members outside the cluster, typically the organization Layer5 Cloud creates for every new account, is deleted. Before it is deleted, an empty workspace (no designs, environments, or views) is soft-deleted, and a non-empty workspace moves, with its ownership, to the canonical account's earliest-created organization. An organization that does have other active members is preserved, and its ownership transfers to the retained account. Related organizations are deleted leaves first, children before parents.

If a connection name collides during the merge, the duplicate is renamed with a `(merged)` suffix, and `(merged, 2)`, `(merged, 3)`, and so on for any further collisions on the same name, so both remain identifiable.

People whose accounts are merged receive no notification.

{{< alert type="info" title="Nothing for you to do" >}}
Customers do not run consolidation. If you sign in with a different method and resources appear to be missing, [contact support]({{< ref "cloud/getting-started/support.md" >}}) with the email addresses you have used to sign in.
{{< /alert >}}

## Signing in with multiple methods

Signing in with email and password, GitHub, or Google using the same **verified** email address always resolves to the same account:

1. You create an account with `alice@example.com`, whether by setting a password or signing in with GitHub or Google.
2. Later, you sign in with a different method (for example, Google instead of GitHub) using a provider that returns the same verified email address.
3. Layer5 Cloud recognizes the verified email address and signs you into your existing account rather than creating a new one.

Your designs, organizations, and workspaces are available regardless of which sign-in method you used to create them. Each email address belongs to a single active account, so a second account can no longer be created for an address that already belongs to one. For how sign-in methods attach to one account, see [Account Linking]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/_index.md#account-linking" >}}).

## Your email addresses

Your account has exactly one **primary** email address at a time. That is the address shown on your profile and the one used to identify you.

If your account absorbed a duplicate during consolidation, Layer5 Cloud also keeps a record of the addresses that duplicate used. Each of those addresses continues to work for:

- Accepting invitations sent to that address
- Role assignments made against that address

These additional addresses are not displayed in the Layer5 Cloud interface. The account holder, or a Provider Admin, can list them through the API at `GET /api/identity/users/{userId}/emails`.

## Wanting separate accounts

Each email address maps to exactly one active account. If you deliberately want separate accounts, for example to keep a testing environment separate from production, use a distinct email address for each account.

## For organization admins: billing impact

The billable user count follows organization membership and counts distinct people, so a person who had several accounts in one organization counts once after the merge. The count is recalculated on its regular schedule and never falls below the plan's minimum number of users. There is nothing to adjust manually.

{{< alert type="info" title="Minimum-seat plans" >}}
Billable seats never drop below your plan's minimum. If your plan was already at its minimum-seat floor, consolidation has no effect on your seat count or billing.
{{< /alert >}}

## Why consolidation is required

A Layer5 Cloud database migration enforces one active account per email address. That migration refuses to apply while duplicate accounts remain, and reports:

> Refusing to enforce email uniqueness: N live duplicate-email cluster(s) remain in users. Run the consolidate-users command (default mode, then --by-email) to clear them first

A second variant of the check refuses when two active entries in the email-address records share one address. Self-hosted operators who upgrade across this migration must run consolidation first. Once the migration applies, Layer5 Cloud cannot create a second active account for an address that already belongs to one.

## How consolidation works

Consolidation runs in four phases: discovery, planning, merging, and linking the identity. Discovery and planning only read data. Merging and linking write only in a live run.

Discovery groups live, non-anonymous accounts that have not already been merged by the identity-provider identity they share. Accounts with no email address are ignored. An account in Pending status joins a cluster only when its email exactly matches an active account already in that cluster. A cluster needs two or more accounts. An active account whose email resolves to no identity, and an email address that maps to more than one identity, are never merged. They are reported for review.

Each cluster keeps one canonical account, in this order: an Active account wins over one that is not, then the earliest-created account, then the account with the lowest id. Every other account in the cluster is retired.

Each cluster merges inside one database transaction:

1. Every duplicate must still be live and unmerged. If any changed since planning, the cluster is skipped with "skipped (already merged / changed since planning)". A skip does not stop the run.
2. Duplicate role assignments the canonical account already holds are soft-deleted. The rest move.
3. Colliding connection names are renamed as described above.
4. Every live record a duplicate owns moves to the canonical account.
5. Organization and team memberships are recomputed inside the transaction. Two memberships duplicate when they share the same organization or team and the same role. A different role in the same scope is kept. When two memberships duplicate, the higher-privilege role wins, ranked from highest: Provider Admin, Organization Admin, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Workspace Manager, Academy Admin, User, Academy Learner. Unknown role names tie, and the older membership wins.
6. Organizations a duplicate owns are deleted or transferred as described in [What changed](#what-changed).
7. Each duplicate's live email-address records are retired, and each distinct address the duplicates used is added to the canonical account as a non-primary address with source `consolidation`.
8. Each duplicate account is soft-deleted, and one audit record is written per duplicate.

After the transaction commits, consolidation records the canonical account on the person's identity-provider identity, so later sign-ins resolve to it. The link is written only when the identity has no linked account yet or is linked to an account in the same cluster. A failed identity link does not undo the merge. Re-running the tool retries the link. A failed merge step rolls back that cluster only and stops the run. Re-running is safe: a finished cluster is a no-op.

## Running it (self-hosted operators)

Prerequisites: the identity-anchor backfill tool has been run, ambiguities from a dry run have been reviewed, a full database backup has been taken, and a separate identity-provider database URL is configured. Without a separate identity-provider URL, the tool falls back to the main database connection, which is valid only in local development where both databases share one instance.

| Flag | Default | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | `true` | Prints the plan and writes nothing. |
| `--yes` | `false` | Confirms writes. A live run needs both `--dry-run=false` and `--yes`. `--yes` alone is still a dry run. `--dry-run=false` without `--yes` aborts with "refusing to run live without --yes; pass --yes to confirm writes, or keep --dry-run". |
| `--limit N` | `0` (all) | Caps the number of clusters processed per run. Ignored with `--cluster`. |
| `--cluster <email or identity id>` | none | Processes one cluster, matched by the canonical account's email, a duplicate's email, or the identity id. |
| `--by-email` | `false` | Residual mode, run after the default mode. Merges duplicate-email clusters that have no identity, or a single identity with no active link, keyed on the shared email. An email shared by more than one identity is skipped and reported. Ignores `--cluster`. |

Run the default mode first, then `--by-email`. Run each as a dry run before running it live.

Each run prints whether it is a dry run or live, the number of clusters and ambiguities, then a plan per cluster or one merge line per cluster. On error, the tool prints `consolidate-users: <error>` and exits with status 1. Apart from a failed identity link, a merge-time error means that cluster's transaction rolled back and the run is safe to repeat. One refusal to know: "Canonical user has no live organization to re-home a non-empty workspace into" means a non-empty workspace needs a destination and the canonical account owns no live organization. "Failed to apply an organization consolidation decision" includes the case where an organization being deleted has a live child organization outside the delete set.

{{< alert type="info" title="Related reading" >}}
For how sign-in providers link to your account, see [Account Linking]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/_index.md#account-linking" >}}).
{{< /alert >}}


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Keys"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keys/index.md
description: Keys are the atomic unit of access control
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In Layer5 Cloud, permissions are represented as keys, each serving as a unique identifier for a specific permission. One or more keys can be grouped together and assigned to a [keychain]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keychains.md" >}}). Then this keychain can be assigned to a [role]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/roles/_index.md" >}}) and that role can be assigned to a user. A user never receives a key directly. This is the general flow of how keys reach a user.

Keys, keychains, and roles are defined once for the whole Layer5 Cloud deployment. They are not copied or customized per organization. What varies per organization is which roles a user holds there. A user's effective keys in an organization are the union of the keys from every role they hold in that organization, so the same person can hold a key in one organization and lack it in another. Holding an additional role only adds keys. It never removes any. Provider Admin holds every key and passes every check in every organization. For how this fits with authentication and cross-organization resource sharing, see [Security Boundaries]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/_index.md#security-boundaries" >}}).

For instance, consider the system-shipped default key `Create Organization`, which corresponds to the permission to create an organization in the Cloud. To create an organization, you need the `Create Organization` key in a keychain that is assigned to a role associated with your user account in that organization.

{{< alert title="Note" >}}

1. The same key can be assigned to multiple keychains.
2. One or more keys can be assigned to a keychain.
3. Keys are deployment-wide. The organization context decides which of your roles, and therefore which keys, apply to a request.

{{< /alert >}}

A default installation ships more than 240 keys grouped into 30 default keychains. The system account owns every default key and keychain.

### Keys Types

Keys follow one of four shapes. A few grant an action that is not a simple change to a resource.

1. **Create** - Create keys permit you to create resources. For example, the `Create Organization` key allows you to create an organization.
2. **View** - View keys permit you to access and retrieve resources. For example, the `View All Teams` key lets you see all the teams within a selected organization.
3. **Edit** - Edit keys permit you to change resources. For instance, the `Edit Organization` key allows you to update an organization's details.
4. **Delete** - Delete keys permit you to remove resources. For instance, the `Delete Token` key allows you to revoke a token.
5. **Action** - Action keys grant a workflow step. For example, the `Approve Catalog Request` key allows you to approve a catalog request to publish a cloud-native design to [Cloud Catalog]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/catalog/_index.md" >}}), and the `Connect GitHub Account to Workspace` key enables you to connect your GitHub account to your [workspace]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/spaces/workspaces.md" >}}).

### Keys Enforcement

A key has an effect only where something checks it. Two places do.

- **The server.** On a guarded action, the server resolves the organization of the request and tests whether the user holds the required key there. A missing key returns HTTP 403 with a JSON body. This check is what actually protects the action.
- **The interface.** The Layer5 Cloud UI reads your effective keys for the organization in context and disables or hides controls for actions you cannot perform. For more on the organization context switcher, see [Organizations]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/organizations/_index.md" >}}).

Not every key is checked in both places. Some security keys are enforced only by the interface: the server does not test Delete Token, and tests Create Token only when you approve a desktop app or CLI sign-in. For that approval, Create Token must be held in at least one organization you belong to. The organization you have selected, or the one a custom domain belongs to, does not matter. Changes to keys, keychains, and roles are checked on the server, which also requires the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. The [security permission keys]({{< ref "cloud/reference/_index.md#permission-keys" >}}) table lists which security keys the server enforces.

Because a key grants nothing unless a check names it, a custom key is only a record. Adding one to a keychain and a role changes no behavior anywhere.

Each key that the interface does check is enforced at specific UI elements. For instance, the `Create Organization` key is enforced at the **Create Organization** button on the **Organizations** page. The button is disabled if you do not hold `Create Organization` through a role in the selected organization.

### Keys Management

#### View Keys

Review keys by navigating to the [Keys](https://cloud.layer5.io/security/keys) page. Every signed-in user can open the Keys tab. It lists the system's keys plus any keys you created, and searches by key name. Viewing keys requires no key on the server.

#### Review Key Usage

Keys themselves do not carry a usage counter. There is no "last used" column on the Keys page. What a key's use leaves behind is the event that the action itself produced, and those events are what you audit.

Every action a user takes is recorded on the [Audit Logs](https://cloud.layer5.io/events/audit) page, which answers who did what, and when:

- **User ID** - the account that performed the action, which is the account whose key was exercised.
- **Category** and **Action** - what was done, for example a workspace being created or a team being deleted. These correspond to the capability the key grants.
- **Acted Upon** - the resource the action was performed on.
- **Description** and **Created At** - the detail of the event and the time it occurred.

Filter by **Actor ID** to follow one user's activity, or by **Category** and **Action** to see everyone who exercised a particular capability over a period. Because keys are evaluated in the context of an organization, the log you are reading is the log for the organization you currently have selected.

Workspaces additionally keep their own activity log, scoped to that one workspace. See [View Recent Activity]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-workspaces/index.md#view-recent-activity" >}}).

Key and keychain changes do not write audit events. Creating, downloading, and deleting a token do. See [Tokens]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/tokens.md" >}}).

#### Assign Keys

Changing which keys a keychain carries, or which keychains a role includes, is a Provider Admin action for the whole deployment. Holding Provider Admin inside one organization does not satisfy that check. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, Layer5 operates the Provider Admin role, so organizations cannot change keys. On a self-hosted deployment, the operator's Provider Admins can.

To grant an existing key to a user, assign a role that already carries it. Do not add the keychain to a shared role unless every holder of that role in every organization should gain it.

1. Select the organization in the organization context switcher in the top navigation bar.
2. Confirm which role already carries the key. The [Default Permissions]({{< ref "cloud/reference/default-permissions.md" >}}) matrix lists the default roles. [Keychains]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keychains.md" >}}) explains how keys are grouped.
3. Open the [Users](https://cloud.layer5.io/identity/users) page and assign that role to the user in this organization. You can also invite a user and assign the role separately. See [Users]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/_index.md" >}}) and [Roles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/roles/_index.md" >}}).

A Provider Admin who needs a new combination of keys creates a keychain, includes it in a role, and then assigns that role. See [Keychains]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keychains.md#create-keychains" >}}).

{{< alert title="Permission Assignment at Teams, Organization and Provider Levels" >}}

1. Team Admin can assign roles to users in a team. Team Admin cannot edit keys or keychains.
2. Organization Admin can assign roles to users in an organization. Organization Admin cannot edit keys or keychains.
3. Only Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete keys, change which keys a keychain carries, or change which keychains a role includes. The server checks that role across the whole deployment.

{{< /alert >}}

### Keys Lifecycle

Layer5 Cloud ships with more than 240 default keys. Default keys are owned by the system. Each key is uniquely identified by a UUID, which is how the system references the key.

Creating or editing a key, including changing which keychains carry it, requires the Edit Key key. Deleting a key requires the Delete Key key. Both belong to the Provider Management keychain, which only Provider Admin holds by default, and the server also requires the caller to hold the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. As of Layer5 Cloud v1.0.280, only a Provider Admin can change keys.

Deleting a key is a soft delete. The key stops granting access immediately and disappears from every keychain that contained it. Because keys are deployment-wide, editing or deleting one changes access for every organization at once.

### Anatomy of a key

The Keys tab lists each key with these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Key ID | A UUID that identifies the key. |
| Name | The action the key grants, for example Create Token. |
| Description | What the action does. |
| Category | The resource the key acts on, for example Token or Keychains. |
| Subcategory | The default keychain family the key belongs to, for example Security Management. |
| Owner | The account that owns the key. Default keys are owned by the system. |
| Created At, Deleted At | When the key was created and, if deleted, when. |

### Who can see and change keys

| Key | Governs | Default holders besides Provider Admin | Enforced by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| View Keys | Seeded for the Keys tab | User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin | Not checked. Every signed-in user sees the Keys tab. |
| Edit Key | Creating and changing a key | None | Interface and server. The server also requires the Provider Admin role. |
| Delete Key | Deleting a key | None | Interface and server. The server also requires the Provider Admin role. |

The list shows system-owned default keys, plus keys you created. Keys are deployment-wide, not per organization.

When the server refuses a change to a key, it answers HTTP 403 with a JSON error. A caller who lacks the route's key receives code `meshery_cloud-1108`. A caller who holds the key but is not a Provider Admin for the whole deployment receives code `meshery_cloud-3336`, "Only a Provider Admin can change roles, keychains or permission keys".

### Tracing a missing permission

When a user cannot perform an action, work from the key outward:

1. Identify the key the action requires. A 403 response or a disabled control both point to a missing key.
2. Find the roles that carry that key in [Default Permissions]({{< ref "cloud/reference/default-permissions.md" >}}). Security keys are listed above and on [Keychains]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keychains.md" >}}), [Sessions]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/sessions.md" >}}), and [Tokens]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/tokens.md" >}}).
3. Check which roles the user holds in the organization the request ran in, not in the organization they usually work in.
4. Grant a role that carries the key in that organization.

### Limits

- Keys do not rotate or expire. A key grants its action until it is deleted or removed from the user's roles.
- Keys have no per-key usage counter. Use the Audit Logs page instead.
- On hosted Layer5 Cloud, only Provider Admins edit or delete keys.
- A key and its keychains are deployment-wide. Organizations tailor access by assigning roles, not by changing keys.

### Key endpoints

Success responses are JSON unless stated. Errors from these handlers return a plain-text message. Refusals from the authorization layer return JSON. Paths sit under `/api`.

| Method and path | Who may call | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /auth/keys` | Signed-in user | Lists keys you can see. Parameters: `page`, `pageSize`, `order`, `search` (matches the key name). Default order: most recently updated first. |
| `GET /auth/keys/{keyId}` | Signed-in user | Returns one key. A malformed id returns `400`. |
| `POST /auth/keys` | Provider Admin holding Edit Key | Creates or updates a key. |
| `DELETE /auth/keys/{keyId}` | Provider Admin holding Delete Key | Soft-deletes the key. Returns `204`. |
| `GET /identity/orgs/{orgId}/users/keys` | Signed-in user | Returns your effective keys in the organization. The interface uses it to enable controls. |

For a Provider Admin, a malformed id on a write returns `400` with a plain-text message. See [Cloud API]({{< ref "cloud/reference/api-reference/_index.md" >}}) for authentication and the organization header.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Using Academy Content Template Creator"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/academy/creating-content/using-content-template-creator/index.md
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Academy Content Template Creator is a step-by-step wizard that helps you create structured templates for your Academy content. This generator streamlines the process of
creating learning paths, challenges, and certifications by collecting all necessary metadata and generating a ready-to-use template.


## Getting Started
![Academy Content Template Creator](images/template-creator.png)
1. Access the Creator: Click on the "Create New Content" card in your Academy dashboard
2. Create Your Content: The wizard will guide you through **5 essential steps** to create your content template

Since it's straightforward, let's walk through a practical example to demonstrate the process.

## Example: Creating "Meshery Contributors Certification"

This example demonstrates how to use the **Academy Content Template Creator** to build a **certification** program for **Meshery contributors**. Each step shows what information to enter, followed by specific example values.

### Step 1: Basic Information
![Step 1: Basic Information](images/template-creator-step1.png)
- Type: Choose "Certification" from Learning Path, Challenge, or Certification
- Title: "Meshery Contributors Certification"
- Description: "A comprehensive certification program for developers looking to become active contributors to Meshery"

### Step 2: Content Details
![Step 2: Content Details](images/template-creator-step2.png)
<!-- - Level: Intermediate (assumes basic cloud-native knowledge) -->
- Categories: "open-source, cloud-native"
- Add Tags: "meshery", "kubernetes", "golang", "contribution", "open-source"
- Banner Image: "images/meshery-contributors-banner.svg"

### Step 3: Content Access
![Step 3: Content Access](images/template-creator-step3.png)
- Workspace: "Meshery Academy"
- Team: "Contributors Program"
- Access Status: Enabled
- Content Access End Date: Leave blank for permanent access (Meshery always welcomes contributors)

**Understanding Access Status: Enabled vs Disabled**

Access status sets the invitation to enabled or disabled. It defaults to enabled. It does not by itself hide the catalog card. New content starts public, not ready, and beginner. Catalog visibility is that public flag. Access status only governs enrollment.

**Enabled:** a signed-in learner can enroll. Enrolling accepts the invitation.

**Disabled:** the invitation blocks enrollment. Learners who already enrolled keep their role and team membership. Their progress is not paused.

**Content Access End Date** is the invitation's expiry. Leave it empty for no expiry. Expiry is checked at enrollment. After it passes, new learners cannot enroll. Learners who already enrolled keep their role and team membership.

The team field accepts one existing team. That team is added to the invitation, and learners join it when they enroll. You can type a new workspace name. The team must already exist.

### Step 4: Recognition
![Step 4: Recognition](images/template-creator-step4.png)

The Recognition step defines the badge or certificate awarded upon completion. You have two options:
- **Use Existing Recognition**: Choose from the Layer5 collection
- **Create New Recognition**: Design a custom badge with an image URL

**For our example:**
- Create a "Meshery Contributor" badge with the Meshery logo


### Step 5: Generate Template
![Step 5: Generate Template](images/template-creator-step5.png)

After clicking "Continue" in Step 4, a success notification appears in the bottom-right corner confirming your template has been created successfully.

{{< alert type="info" title="Navigation Between Steps" >}}
You can navigate back to any previous step to make modifications. When you return to earlier steps and make changes, your entries in the subsequent steps will remain intact.
{{< /alert >}}


**Generated Template Output for Meshery Contributors Certification:**

This template provides the YAML front matter metadata for static site generators (like Hugo/Jekyll). After copying it, we can directly create new content files in our Academy repository.

```yaml
---
type: "certification"
title: "Meshery Contributors Certification"
description: "A comprehensive certification program for developers looking to become active contributors to Meshery"
weight: 1
banner: "images/meshery-contributors-banner.svg"
id: "unique-content-id"
level: "beginner"
---

Provide a brief summary of what learners will gain.
<!-- Add your Academy content here -->
```

{{< alert type="info" title="Important Reference IDs" >}}
Make note of two key identifiers for your content files:
- **Content ID**: Unique identifier for this specific content
- **Organization ID**: Your organization's identifier (remains constant)
{{< /alert >}}

The `level` key in this output always reads `beginner`, whatever difficulty you picked on Content Details. Set it to `beginner`, `intermediate`, or `advanced` yourself. The creator also includes `tags` and `categories` when you entered them, and commented `competencies` and `prerequisite_knowledge` samples you can uncomment. `weight` is fixed at `1` until you change it.

{{< alert type="info" title="Content ID Updates" >}}
The creator writes the record when you advance from Recognition to Generate Template. You can go back and your entries stay, but advancing to the last step again creates another record with a new content ID and a new invitation. Use the ID on the final screen of your last run, and treat any earlier record as unused.
{{< /alert >}}

### Next Steps

After generating our template:

1. **Copy the Template**: Use the provided copy button to get your front matter
2. **Create Your Content File**: Paste the template into a new .md file in your academy repository
3. **Add Your Content**: Replace the placeholder comment with your actual learning material


## Manage Invitation

### Auto-Generated Invitations
Navigate to **Identity → Invitations** to find your automatically created invitation.
![](images/auto-invitation.png)

The first column labeled "INVITATION" contains a shareable link that you can copy.

## What Can the Invitation Link Do for You?

The auto-generated invitation link is a powerful tool that helps instructors efficiently manage learner access and streamline the enrollment process.

### 1. What accepting the invitation does

Enrolling accepts the invitation. Acceptance is where access is decided.

- **Team**: The learner is added to the one team you picked, if they are not already a member. The creator does not assign several teams.
- **Role**: Academy Learner is assigned in the organization if the learner does not already hold it.
- **Who can accept**: The email list starts empty, so anyone who is signed in can accept. The invitation is not limited to people already in your organization, and it does not email the team for you. Add exact addresses or `@domain` entries on the invitation to restrict who can accept. See [User Invitations]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/user-invitations/index.md" >}}).

### 2. Sharing the link

Copy the invitation link from the invitation list and send it yourself. The link registers a learner for the content by accepting that invitation. It does not send mail on its own.


### Customize Invitation Properties

Click the pencil icon to access the invitation customization form.
![](images/auto-invitation-details.png)

The invitation form contains eight properties. Three are automatically generated by the system for convenience, which you can modify according to your needs:

**Auto-Generated Properties:**
1. **Name**: `Academy Invitation for <slug>`, using the generated slug, not the title you typed.
2. **Description**: Identifies the organization and the curricula the invitation is for.
3. **Roles**: Defaults to Academy Learner. [Academy roles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/roles/academy-roles/index.md" >}}) lists what that role can do. Empty quota means unlimited acceptances, and the invitation counts each person once.

{{< alert type="info" title="Admin Role Invitations" >}}
Academy admins can invite other instructors to become co-admins by changing the **Roles** property from "Academy Learner" to "Academy Admin" during invitation customization.
{{< /alert >}}

**Customizable Properties:**

### 1. Emails - Invitation Email List

The email list restricts who may accept. It starts empty, and an empty list lets any signed-in user accept. It does not send the invitation for you.

- **Supported Formats:**
  - Individual emails: `test@domain.com`
  - Domain entries: `@domain.com` (only addresses at that domain may accept)
- **Duplicate Handling**: The system automatically merges duplicate entries
- **Quantity Recommendations:**
  - Small team invitations: 10-50 email addresses
  - Department-level invitations: 100-200 email addresses
  - Large organizations: Use domain wildcards like `@company.com` instead of listing individual emails

### 2. Expires At - Expiration Settings

Control when the invitation expires:

- **Flexibility**: Supports any time setting, extension, and recovery. Leave blank for permanent access
- **What happens at expiration?**
  - Expiration is only checked when users attempt to accept the invitation
  - If the expiration time has passed, users cannot proceed with the invitation
  - Expiration check compares server current time vs. set expiration time
- **Can I modify expired invitations?**
  - Yes, you can recover and extend expiration times by entering edit mode

### 3. Quota - Usage Limits

Set limits on how many users can accept the invitation:

- **When quota is exceeded:**
  - Operates on a first-accept, first-in basis
  - Users beyond the quota cannot join, even with a valid invitation link
- **Recovery options:**
  - If quota is reached, you can increase the quota to restore access
  - Admin console provides real-time usage monitoring

### 4. Teams - Team Assignment List

Specify which teams invited users will join:

- **Team Selection**: Choose one existing team. The creator accepts a single team, and learners join that team when they enroll.
- **No Teams Available**: If your organization has no teams, [create one]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/teams/_index.md" >}}) first.

{{< alert type="info" title="Team Structure Changes" >}}
**During Organization Restructuring:**
- If team structure changes after invitations are sent
- Some teams may be merged or deleted
- New users can still join remaining valid teams

**Permission Management Updates:**
- Team permission policies may change
- Some teams might close to new users
- Other teams continue accepting new members normally
{{< /alert >}}

### 5. Status - Enabled/Disabled

Control invitation accessibility:

- **Enabled**: Enrollment can accept the invitation.
- **Disabled**: Enrollment fails. Learners who already enrolled are not removed.

{{< alert type="info" title="Invitation Idempotency" >}}
Acceptance is idempotent. A learner who accepts twice gains no duplicate membership or role, and the invitation counts them once.
{{< /alert >}}

When an enrollment hits a disabled, expired, full, or email-restricted invitation, the request fails with a server error. The registration is recorded before the invitation is evaluated, so the learner can appear in the Learners view without having joined the organization or the team. Fix the invitation, then have the learner enroll again.

Content created while the console is scoped to all organizations belongs to the provider organization. It has no attached invitation, so enrollment accepts nothing and grants no team or role.

You can change the team, access status, and end date later from the Curricula view of the [Instructor Console]({{< ref "cloud/academy/creating-content/instructor-console-guide/index.md" >}}). To bring in a co-instructor, create an invitation with the Academy Admin role instead of Academy Learner.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Workspaces"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/concepts/spaces/workspaces/index.md
description: Understand the core concepts of Workspaces.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A workspace is a named grouping inside an organization. It brings together the teams who do a piece of work, the environments they deploy to, and the designs and views they work on. A workspace does two separate jobs:

- **It organizes resources.** Designs and views live in a workspace, and the workspace decides which organization they are listed under.
- **It grants connection access.** Assigning a team to a workspace gives that team's members read-only access to the connections in the workspace's environments. That is the only access a team assignment grants.

You can create Workspaces to group related Designs and Environments and to decide which teams can read which connections.

## Key Features

- **Connection access:** Assigning a team grants read-only access to the connections, and their credentials, in the workspace's environments.
- **Logical Grouping:** Within Workspaces, you can group related environments, designs, and views.
- **Organization-wide visibility:** Every member of an organization can list and open every workspace in that organization. Team assignment does not narrow what you see.
- **One design, one workspace:** A design or view belongs to at most one workspace. Assigning it moves it.
- **The last workspace stays:** An organization always keeps at least one workspace.

### Workspace Relationships and Restrictions

- Every member of the organization can list and open every workspace. Team membership does not hide workspaces.
- A workspace may have zero or more environments. Creating a workspace assigns no team and no environment.
- A team assignment grants read-only access to connections in those environments. It does not grant access to designs or views.
- One or more teams can be assigned to a workspace, and the same team can be assigned to more than one workspace. The team must belong to the workspace's organization.

After creating a Workspace, assign teams, move designs into the Workspace, and associate one or more Environments so those Environments' connections become readable by the workspace's teams.

Like a shared drive (or shared collection of files), Workspaces are your Google Drive, while Designs are your Google Docs.

## Key Workspace Components

### Environments

- Environments are a central part of a workspace. They serve as a logical grouping for managing connections. A connection, in this context, can be either managed or discovered. Examples of connections include Kubernetes clusters, Prometheus instances, Jaeger traces, Nginx servers, and more.
- One or more environments can be assigned to a workspace.
- Same environment can be assigned to multiple workspaces.

{{< alert type="info" title="Assigning Environments to Workspaces" >}}
Assign any number of Environments to one or more Workspaces. See [Environments]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/spaces/environments.md" >}}) section for more information.
{{< /alert >}}

### Profiles

- A profile represents a person or persona in the organization and groups the connections it publishes through.
- Assigning a profile to a workspace makes it visible to the members of the workspace's teams.
- The same profile can be assigned to multiple workspaces. See [Profiles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/spaces/profiles.md" >}}).

### Designs

- A design or view belongs to at most one workspace. Assigning it to a workspace is a move, not a copy: Layer5 Cloud removes every earlier workspace assignment, then adds the new one.
- The workspace a design sits in decides the organization under which the design is listed, and the organization in which the Share Design permission is checked.
- Placing a private design in a workspace does not open it to the workspace's teams. Share the design to give someone access. See [Sharing Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/designer/sharing/index.md" >}}).
- When you list the designs you can add to a workspace, the list shows only designs you own that are not already in it.
- Moving a design requires the Assign Designs to Workspaces permission in the destination workspace's organization. Layer5 Cloud does not also require access to the workspace the design leaves.

{{< alert type="info" title="Design Ownership in Workspaces" >}}
Designs belong to only one Workspace at any given time. Ownership does not change when a design moves. See [Designs](https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/designs) section for more information.
{{< /alert >}}

### Teams

- A Workspace is closely associated with Teams. Teams are groups of users with varying permissions, and they are at the center of resource access and management within a Workspace.
- One or more teams can be assigned to a workspace.
- Same team can be assigned to multiple workspaces.

{{< alert type="info" title="Team Access Control in Workspaces" >}}
Team assignment grants read-only access to the connections in the workspace's environments. It does not grant access to designs, and it does not decide who can see the workspace. See [Teams]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/teams/_index.md" >}}).
{{< /alert >}}

### Connections

- Connections refer to various resources that can be either managed or unmanaged, but are discovered and made accessible for use. Examples of Connections include Kubernetes clusters, Prometheus instances, Jaeger services, Nginx deployments, and more. These Connections serve as a fundamental part of Workspaces, as users can deploy infrastructure designs within the context of these Connections.
- Connections can be assigned to one or more environments.
- Same connection can be assigned to multiple environments.

{{< alert type="info" title="Learn More About Connections" >}}
See [Connections](https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/logical/connections) section for more information.
{{< /alert >}}

## Best Practices

To make the most of Workspaces, here are some best practices:

- Clearly define permissions in the form of team assignment to ensure proper access control.
- Use Infrastructure Designs to standardize resource deployments.
- Regularly review and update your Workspace's resources and configurations.

Workspaces enhance collaboration within your teams, providing a structured environment for sharing and managing resources. By following best practices and understanding the core components of Workspaces, you can maximize the benefits of this feature.

{{< alert type="info" title="Looking for Practical Workspace Management?" >}}
For a step-by-step guide on how to create, edit, and manage your workspaces, see the [Managing Workspaces]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-workspaces/index.md" >}}) documentation.
{{< /alert >}}

## Example: Orbital Labs Workspace Setup

The following illustrates how Five and Maya set up workspaces at Orbital Labs to segment access across infrastructure and development workflows. See [Meet Five and the Cast]({{< ref "cloud/getting-started/meet-five/_index.md" >}}) for the full seed inventory.

### Workspace Inventory

| Workspace | Owner Org | Teams with Access | Environments |
|---|---|---|---|
| `orbital-production` | Orbital Labs | Infrastructure only | `prod-aws` (EKS + RDS + S3 + CloudFront + SQS), `prod-gcp` (GKE + Cloud SQL + Cloud Storage + Pub/Sub) |
| `orbital-staging` | Orbital Labs | Infrastructure + Development | `staging-aws` (EKS + S3 + ElastiCache), `staging-azure` (AKS + Azure Blob + Azure Service Bus) |
| `orbital-dev` | Orbital Labs | Development only | `dev-local` (kind + LocalStack) |

### Creating orbital-staging

Five creates the `orbital-staging` workspace to give the Development team a shared environment for feature-branch testing  -  without handing them the keys to production.

**Steps Five follows:**
1. Navigate to **Workspaces** and click **Create Workspace**
2. Name the workspace `orbital-staging`
3. Save  -  the workspace is created with no team access and no environments assigned

**Maya then assigns team access:**
1. Open the `orbital-staging` workspace settings
2. Add the **Infrastructure** team so its members can read the connections in the workspace's environments
3. Add the **Development** team so its members can read those same connections

{{< alert type="info" title="Why both teams?" >}}
Assigning a team grants read-only connection access, not design access. Infrastructure and Development can both read the staging connections. Development still cannot read production connections, because it is not assigned to `orbital-production`. To let Rex or Jordan open a private design, share that design with them.
{{< /alert >}}

## Organization-wide visibility

Workspace visibility is organization-wide. Every member of an organization can list and open every workspace in that organization, whether or not one of their teams is assigned to it. The Workspaces, Environments, and connection areas of the Cloud UI appear only to people who hold the matching View Workspace, View Environment, and View Connections permissions.

A workspace belongs to exactly one organization for its whole life. Editing a workspace changes its name, description, or metadata, never its organization.

## What a team assignment grants

A member of a team reaches a connection through four live links. Breaking any one of them ends the access.

| Link | Created by | Broken by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. User is a member of a team | Adding the user to the team | Removing the user from the team |
| 2. Team is assigned to a workspace | Assign team to workspace | Removing the team from the workspace, or deleting the workspace |
| 3. Environment is assigned to the workspace | Assign environment to workspace | Removing the environment from the workspace, or deleting either one |
| 4. Connection is assigned to the environment | Assign connections to environment | Removing the connection from the environment, or deleting the environment |

The result is read-only. Modifying or deleting a connection still requires owning it. Two other routes reach a connection independently of this chain: owning it, and holding the View All Organizations key. See [Environments]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/spaces/environments.md" >}}).

## One workspace per design

Because a design sits in at most one workspace, promotion from one workspace to another is a move. There is no approval step and no copy. The same rule applies to views. Removing a design from its workspace leaves it with no workspace. The design and its owner are unaffected.

## The last workspace

Every organization receives a workspace when it is created, so designs always have somewhere to live. Layer5 Cloud creates **My Workspace** in any organization that has no workspace.

An organization always keeps at least one workspace. Deleting the last one is refused with `cannot delete workspace: at least one workspace must exist for the organization`. Two simultaneous deletes cannot both succeed and leave the organization empty.

Deleting a workspace ends every team, environment, design, and view assignment it holds, in one step. The teams, environments, designs, views, and connections themselves remain. Designs and views that were in the workspace are left in no workspace until you assign them to another one. Team members lose any connection access that flowed through the deleted workspace.

## Names, edits, and activity

A name and description are each limited to 255 characters. Names are not unique: two workspaces in one organization can share a name. An edit changes only the fields you send.

Each workspace records an activity log: creating, editing, and deleting the workspace, and assigning or removing teams, environments, designs, and views. Every entry carries the email address of the person who acted. Reading the log requires the View Workspace permission.

## Permissions

Every workspace action is checked in the organization that owns the workspace. Creating a workspace is checked in the organization you create it in. The keys are View Workspace, Create Workspace, Edit Workspace, Delete Workspace, Assign team to workspace, Remove team from workspace, Assign environment to workspace, Remove environment from workspace, Assign Designs to Workspaces, Remove Designs from Workspaces, Assign Views to Workspace, and Unassign Views from Workspace. Default holders are in [Default Permissions]({{< ref "cloud/reference/default-permissions.md" >}}).

Layer5 Cloud enforces no plan check on workspace actions. Creating, editing, deleting, and assigning work the same on every plan, governed only by those permissions.

## Related

- [Managing Workspaces]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-workspaces/index.md" >}}) covers creating, editing, and deleting workspaces and assigning their members.
- [Environments]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/spaces/environments.md" >}}) explains the deploy targets a workspace exposes.
- [Promote a Design]({{< ref "cloud/guides/tutorials/promoting-a-design.md" >}}) moves a design from a staging workspace to a production workspace.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Sessions"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/sessions/index.md
description: User sessions are created each time a user successfully authenticates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What sessions are

A session is the credential Layer5 Cloud issues each time someone signs in. It is what keeps a browser tab, a second device, or a connected Meshery Server signed in, and it is what you end when you want one of those sign-ins to stop working. Sessions expire on their own. [API tokens]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/tokens.md" >}}) do not.

Layer5 Cloud sessions use [OAuth 2.0](https://oauth.net/2/) for authentication. OAuth 2.0 is a standard protocol for authorization and focuses on client developer simplicity while providing specific authorization flows for web applications, desktop applications, mobile phones, and so on.

These are the Layer5 Cloud deployment defaults. Operators of a self-hosted deployment can change them.

| Credential | Default lifetime | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Access token | 24 hours | The browser session ends when it lapses. Activity in the interface does not extend it, so a browser user signs in again after 24 hours. |
| Refresh token | 1000 hours (about 41 days) | Clients such as Meshery Server use it to obtain a new access token. Each refresh token works once. Every refresh issues a new one. A failed refresh returns an error. |
| Sign-in flow | 12 hours | Time allowed to complete a sign-in. |
| Privileged-action window | Set by the deployment; 15 minutes in the packaged default | Sensitive actions, such as profile changes, ask you to authenticate again once this window has passed since sign-in. |
| Anonymous Kanvas session | 24 hours | For use without signing in. It does not appear on the Sessions tab. |

The browser keeps the session in the `provider_token` cookie. Page scripts cannot read it (HttpOnly), it is sent only over HTTPS, and it uses SameSite Lax, so other sites cannot send it along with their own requests except on ordinary top-level navigation. A second cookie, `has_session`, tells the interface that a session exists. It carries no secret, page scripts can read it, and it lapses with the session.

## Creating and using sessions

Every sign-in creates its own session. Each browser, device, and Meshery Server that signs in through Layer5 Cloud holds a separate session with its own expiry, and any number of them can be active at once. Ending one session leaves the others untouched.

A session acts as the user who signed in. What it can do in an organization is whatever the roles that user holds there allow, checked on every request. See [Keys]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keys.md" >}}) for how roles grant permissions.

To use a session, sign in to your Layer5 Cloud user account. The session cookie is stored in that browser. Use the same browser until the session expires. You can have multiple sessions active concurrently, on the same device or on different devices. Each session receives its own authentication token and expiry time.

It is possible to use the same account from two sessions at once. For example, you may open the same Kanvas design in two sessions and see your avatar twice in the design, along with your mouse cursor. You can use this to collaborate with yourself or with others.

Users see their own sessions on the [Sessions](https://cloud.layer5.io/security/sessions) tab of the Security page. Each row shows the session's ID, name, purpose, and creation date. The tab requires the View Sessions key, which every default user role holds. The list shows no device, browser, or location for a session. Search filters by name or purpose, and the newest sessions appear first.

## Revoking sessions

A session ends in one of three ways:

- **Expiry.** The access token lapses at its lifetime. Activity does not extend it.
- **Logout from the Sessions tab.** The session's token is revoked immediately. The next request that presents it fails. The action records the same audit event as deleting a token: `<email> revoked token <name>` (category token, action delete). The confirmation reads `Token "<name>" deleted`, because a session is stored as a token.
- **Signing out of the app.** Signing out ends the browser's identity session and revokes its stored grant.

Changing your password does not end your other sessions. Layer5 Cloud has no sign-out-everywhere action and no idle timeout setting. To end your other sessions, log each one out from the Sessions tab.

The deleted session cannot be restored. Whoever used it must sign in again.

{{< alert type="info" title="Who can use Logout" >}}
The Logout action on the Sessions tab requires the Delete Token key, which only Organization Admins and Provider Admins hold by default. Users, Team Admins, and Workspace Admins see Logout disabled, even though their roles hold the Logout from a Session key. Layer5 Cloud lets each user log out only their own sessions. No role can end another user's session from this tab. The server deletes only your own tokens. Delete Token is enforced by the interface for this control. The server does not test the Delete Token key on the delete request.
{{< /alert >}}

See [Sessions](https://cloud.layer5.io/security/sessions) in Layer5 Cloud.

## If you suspect your account is compromised

1. End every session you do not recognize. A creation date you cannot account for means someone else signed in with your credentials.
2. Change your password. Changing the password does not end other sessions, so complete step 1 first and check the list again afterward.
3. Review your [API tokens]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/tokens.md" >}}) and revoke any you did not create. Tokens never expire and are not sessions, so signing out does not revoke them.
4. If you cannot sign in, ask an Organization Admin or Provider Admin to help recover the account.

Layer5 Cloud has no "sign out everywhere" action. End each session from the list.

## How the browser stores a session

| Cookie | Purpose | Attributes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `provider_token` | The browser session credential | HttpOnly, Secure over HTTPS, SameSite Lax |
| `has_session` | Tells the interface a session exists. Carries no secret and cannot authenticate a request. | Readable by page scripts, SameSite Lax, expires with the session |

The cookie's scope depends on how the organization signs users in:

- **Platform sign-in provider.** The cookie is shared across the platform's hosts, so one sign-in covers them.
- **Organization's own identity provider, or a custom domain outside the platform's domain.** The cookie is host-only and is never sent to any other host.

See [Organizations]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/organizations/_index.md" >}}) for how custom domains and identity providers decide where a user signs in.

## Sessions and API tokens

Sessions and API tokens both authenticate as you, and Layer5 Cloud revokes them through the same mechanism. They differ in how they start and how long they live. Tokens and sessions share one store. `isOauth=false` selects API tokens and `isOauth=true` selects sessions.

| | Session | API token |
|---|---|---|
| Created by | Signing in from a browser, device, or Meshery Server | Creating it on the Tokens tab with a name and purpose |
| Lifetime | 24-hour access token, renewable by clients for up to about 41 days | No expiry |
| Ended by | Expiry, Logout on the Sessions tab, or signing out | Deleting it on the Tokens tab |
| Used for | Interactive use and connected Meshery Servers | Scripts and API clients sending a Bearer token |

The Tokens tab never lists sessions, and the Sessions tab never lists API tokens.

You see only your own sessions. Sessions are scoped to your user account, not to one organization.

## What Layer5 Cloud does not offer

- No organization-level session policy. Lifetimes are set for the whole deployment.
- No idle timeout setting in the product interface.
- No device, browser, or location detail on a session.
- No action that ends every session at once.

## Session endpoints

Paths sit under `/api` unless noted. A missing or revoked credential returns `401` with `{"message": "user must be logged in to perform this operation"}`. When Layer5 Cloud cannot read the revocation record, it refuses the request rather than accept a token it cannot check.

| Method and path | Who may call | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /identity/tokens?isOauth=true` | Signed-in user | Lists your sessions. Default order: newest first. `search` matches name and purpose. The response never contains token values. |
| `DELETE /identity/tokens?tokenId=` | Token owner | Revokes the session. A malformed id returns `400` with `invalid token id`. An unknown or already-deleted id returns `400` with `tokens does not exist`. Writes a delete event. |
| `POST /refresh` (outside `/api`) | Holder of a refresh token | Exchanges a refresh token for a new session credential. Returns `400` with a JSON `error` if the token is missing, malformed, or already used. |
| `GET /logout` (outside `/api`) | Signed-in browser | Ends the browser's identity session. |

| Key | Governs | Default holders besides Provider Admin | Enforced by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| View Sessions | The Sessions tab | User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin | Interface |
| Logout from a Session | Seeded for ending a session | User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin | Not checked. The interface uses Delete Token for Logout. |
| Delete Token | The Logout control on the Sessions tab, and revoking a token | Organization Admin | Interface only. The server deletes only your own tokens. |


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Tokens"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/tokens/index.md
description: API Tokens are used to authenticate to Layer5 Cloud's REST API. Generated on your user account's security tokens page. Tokens can be revoked at any time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What tokens are

An API token lets software act as you. Scripts, CI/CD pipelines, `mesheryctl`, and other Meshery clients present it to Layer5 Cloud instead of signing in through a browser. Because a token carries your full authority and never expires, deciding how many tokens to create, who holds them, and when to delete them is a security decision.

A token is a credential bound to your user account. A client sends it as a bearer token in the `Authorization` header of each request. The [Cloud API reference]({{< ref "cloud/reference/api-reference/_index.md" >}}) shows the exact form.

A token is not scoped to an organization. One token reaches every organization you belong to. Each request chooses the organization it runs in, so a single pipeline token can act in several organizations if you are a member of each.
