See [Specifying Organization Context]({{< ref "cloud/reference/api-reference/_index.md#specifying-organization-context" >}}).

Layer5 Cloud does not record permissions inside the token. It evaluates your roles at the moment of each call, in the organization of that request. There are no token scopes. You cannot limit a token to read-only access, to one organization, or to a subset of your permissions. To give automation narrower authority, give it a token from an account whose roles are narrower.

{{< alert type="info" title="API Tokens are User-Scoped, Not Organization-Scoped" >}}
Layer5 Cloud API tokens are scoped to your user account, not to a specific organization. This means a single API token provides access to all organizations you are a member of, similar to how [GitHub Personal Access Tokens](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens) work. For users who belong to multiple organizations, see [Specifying Organization Context]({{< ref "cloud/reference/api-reference/_index.md#specifying-organization-context" >}}) in the REST API documentation to learn how to control which organization your API requests operate on.
{{< /alert >}}

## Access tokens

Layer5 Cloud REST API uses [OAuth 2.0](https://oauth.net/2/) access tokens for authentication and authorization. Access tokens are opaque tokens that conform to the OAuth 2.0 framework. They are used to authenticate requests to Layer5 APIs and are associated with a user account.

Tokens never expire. Layer5 Cloud offers no expiry setting, and a token remains valid until it is deleted. This differs from [sessions]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/sessions.md" >}}), which Layer5 Cloud creates at each sign-in and which lapse on their own. A token is the right credential for unattended automation. A session is the right one for a person at a browser.

- **Role changes apply at once.** When an administrator grants or removes a role, the next request made with your token reflects the change.
- **Removing the user ends the token.** If your account is disabled or deleted, Layer5 Cloud refuses every request that presents your tokens.

## Creating tokens

You can create a token for your user account at any time. Tokens never expire, but can be revoked. Every token has a name, which is required. The Tokens tab also asks for a purpose. Both are labels. They appear in your token list and help you recognize each token later, and they have no effect on what the token can do. Name the consumer (for example, `ci-snapshots`) and state what it does in the purpose.

Layer5 Cloud creates the token for your user account. It has no expiry and no scope settings. The list shows the ID, name, purpose, and creation date. It never shows the token value. The list is searchable and sortable, and shows the newest tokens first by default.

See [Tokens](https://cloud.layer5.io/security/tokens) in Layer5 Cloud.

### Before you start

- You need the **Create Token** permission to create a token in the interface. User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin hold it by default. A user without it sees the create control disabled.
- You need **View Tokens** to open the Tokens tab. Every default user role holds it.
- Decide which consumer gets this token. Create one token per consumer so you can revoke one without breaking the others.

Open the Tokens tab under Security and start a new token. Enter a name and a purpose.

## Using tokens

To use a token to authenticate to Layer5 Cloud's REST API, pass the token as a Bearer token in the Authorization header of your HTTP request:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "X-Current-Orgid: <organization-id>" \
  https://cloud.layer5.io/api/environments
```

The token authenticates you, not an organization. It reaches every organization you belong to. Name the organization for each request with the `X-Current-Orgid` header. Layer5 Cloud reads that header name only. See [Specifying Organization Context]({{< ref "cloud/reference/api-reference/_index.md#specifying-organization-context" >}}).

What the token can do equals what you can do in that organization. If your role changes, the token's reach changes on the next request.

For GitHub Actions, store the token as a repository secret. See [Use GitHub Actions]({{< ref "cloud/guides/integrations/github-actions/_index.md" >}}).

## Deleting tokens

Deleting a token is how you revoke it. Revocation takes effect immediately and cannot be undone. A deleted token cannot be downloaded again, and every request that presents it fails. There is no way to restore a deleted token. Anything still authenticating with it will start failing, so replace it with a newly created token first if it is in use.

Layer5 Cloud checks revocation on every request. If it cannot complete that check, it refuses the request rather than accept a token that might be revoked.

To delete a token:

1. Go to the [Tokens](https://cloud.layer5.io/security/tokens) page in Layer5 Cloud. Each row shows the token's **ID**, **Name**, **Purpose**, and **Creation Date**.
2. Find the token you want to remove. The list is searchable and sortable, and shows the newest tokens first by default.
3. Click the **trash can** icon in that row's **Actions** column.
4. Confirm in the **Delete Token** dialog, which names the token it is about to delete. Click **Proceed**.

A confirmation notification reports the deleted token by name. The deletion appears as an event in your audit log.

You can delete only your own tokens. The server does not let another user, including a Provider Admin, delete a token for its owner. The owner of a leaked token must revoke it.

{{< alert type="info" title="Permissions Required" >}}
Deleting a token in the interface requires the **Delete Token** key, which Organization Admin and Provider Admin hold by default. Without it the trash can icon is disabled. See [Keys]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keys.md" >}}).
{{< /alert >}}

{{< alert type="info" title="Sessions Are Deleted the Same Way" >}}
Your browser sign-ins are represented by their own tokens and are listed on the [Sessions](https://cloud.layer5.io/security/sessions) page rather than here. There the same action is presented as **Logout** instead of Delete, and it ends that session. See [Sessions]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/sessions.md" >}}).
{{< /alert >}}

{{< alert title="Permissions are enforced by the interface" >}}
The interface requires Create Token, Delete Token, and Download Token. The Layer5 Cloud server accepts requests to create and delete your own tokens without checking those keys. The restriction is current behavior, not a security boundary. See [security permission keys]({{< ref "cloud/reference/_index.md#permission-keys" >}}).
{{< /alert >}}

## Get the token value

Download the token from its row in the list. This needs the **Download Token** permission, which User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin hold by default.

The download is a JSON file named `token_<id>.json` in the format Meshery clients read:

```json
{
  "meshery-provider": "Layer5",
  "token": "<token>"
}
```

You can download a live token again at any time. A revoked token cannot be downloaded. Treat the file like a password: put the `token` value in your CI secret store and delete the file. Anyone who obtains the file can act as you.

The token list never shows a token's value. Creating, downloading, and deleting a token each write an audit event, so your organization's audit trail records who generated a token, who retrieved it, and who revoked it.

## List your tokens over the API

A script can list the tokens your account holds, for example to find old ones before rotating:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/identity/tokens?purpose=ci-snapshots"
```

The answer lists each token's ID, name, purpose, and creation date, never its value. `purpose` keeps only tokens created with exactly that purpose, matched case-sensitively. Leave it out to list every token. `search` matches part of a name or purpose. The list holds API tokens unless you send `isOauth=true`, which lists sign-in sessions instead.

Desktop clients that sign in through Layer5 Cloud create their token with the client's name as its purpose, so the same filter lists the tokens a client created for itself.

## Rotate a token

To rotate a token without downtime, create the replacement first, switch each consumer to it, then delete the old token.

Rotate on a schedule you set, and whenever a person with access to the secret leaves. Layer5 Cloud has no built-in rotation, so rotate in three steps:

1. Create a new token for the same consumer.
2. Update the consumer to use the new token and confirm it works.
3. Revoke the old token.

Revoking last keeps the consumer running the whole time. Revoke at once if a token value leaked.

## Who can manage tokens by default

Each action on the Tokens tab is governed by a [key]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keys.md" >}}). Provider Admin holds every key. With the default roles:

- **View Tokens**, which opens the Tokens tab, is held by every default user role.
- **Download Token** is held by User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, and Organization Admin.
- **Create Token** is held by User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin.
- **Delete Token** is held by Organization Admin and Provider Admin only. For every other role, the interface disables the delete control.

Every token action applies only to your own tokens. You cannot list, download, or delete another user's token. The list shows your own tokens and never the token value.

Roles that hold the keys come from the default keychains: View Tokens sits in User View, Delete Token in Security Management, and Create Token and Download Token in Security Management and User Edit.

{{< alert type="warning" title="Current behavior: token create and delete requests are not checked against the keys" >}}
The Layer5 Cloud server allows any signed-in user to create and delete their own tokens through the API. It does not check the Create Token or Delete Token keys on those requests. Withholding those keys hides the controls in the interface. It does not prevent a user from minting a token. Approving a desktop app or CLI sign-in is different: the server requires Create Token in at least one organization you belong to. The organization you have selected, or the one a custom domain belongs to, does not matter, so a member of a child organization can approve a sign-in on its parent's custom domain.
{{< /alert >}}

A Provider Admin can mint a token on behalf of another account. That token appears in the account holder's token list, and the account holder can revoke it.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The create control is disabled | You lack Create Token in the selected organization. | Ask an Organization Admin to create the token or to grant the key through a role. |
| `401` with "user must be logged in to perform this operation" | The token was revoked, is malformed, or the header is wrong. | Check the header reads `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. If it does, create a new token. |
| `403` on a specific action | You lack the permission for that action in the organization named by `X-Current-Orgid`. | Check your role in that organization. See [Default Permissions]({{< ref "cloud/reference/default-permissions.md" >}}). |
| A token worked before and now fails | The token was revoked, or its owner account was removed. | Create a new token from an active account and replace it in the consumer. |

## Practices that limit risk

- **Create one token per consumer.** A separate token for each pipeline, script, or Meshery Server lets you revoke one without breaking the others.
- **Name each token after its consumer.** The name is the only way to tell tokens apart in the list.
- **Delete a token when its consumer is retired.** A token never expires, so an unused token remains a live credential until you delete it.

Manage your tokens at [cloud.layer5.io/security/tokens](https://cloud.layer5.io/security/tokens).

## Token endpoints

Paths sit under `/api` unless noted. Success responses are JSON unless stated. A missing or revoked credential returns `401` with `{"message": "user must be logged in to perform this operation"}`. When Layer5 Cloud cannot read the revocation record, it refuses the request rather than accept a token it cannot check.

| Method and path | Who may call | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /identity/tokens?name=&purpose=` | Signed-in user | Creates a token for the caller. `name` is required: an empty name returns `400` with `Token name missing.` `purpose` is optional. Writes a create event. |
| `GET /identity/tokens?isOauth=` | Signed-in user | Lists your tokens or sessions. Default order: newest first. `search` matches name and purpose. `purpose` matches exactly, case-sensitively. The response never contains token values. `isOauth=false` selects API tokens. `isOauth=true` selects sessions. |
| `GET /identity/tokens/{id}` | Token owner | Returns the token for download. Returns `404` for an unknown or revoked token and `400` for a malformed id. Writes a download event. |
| `DELETE /identity/tokens?tokenId=` | Token owner | Revokes the token or session. A malformed id returns `400` with `invalid token id`. An unknown or already-deleted id returns `400` with `tokens does not exist`. Writes a delete event. |
| `GET /identity/tokens/infinite?userId=&provider=` | Provider Admin | Issues a non-expiring token for another account. The token is listed under that account. Others receive `403`. |

## Audit events

| Action | Event |
| --- | --- |
| Create a token | `<email> generated token <name>` (category token, action create) |
| Download a token | `Token <name> downloaded` (category token, action download). A failed download is also recorded, with an error severity. |
| Delete a token or log out a session | `<email> revoked token <name>` (category token, action delete) |


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Notification Preferences"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/notification-preferences/index.md
description: Manage your notifications on Layer5 Cloud
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Layer5 Cloud sends email when something happens that involves you: you earn a badge, your role changes, someone comments on your design. Notification preferences decide which of those emails reach you. Preferences belong to your account, so they apply in every organization you belong to.

Email is the only channel. Layer5 Cloud has no per-event choice between email and another channel.

You need the **View Profile** permission, which the default user role holds. The preferences are on your own account, and you cannot set them for anyone else.

## To change the notification preferences

1. Sign into [Layer5 Cloud](https://cloud.layer5.io).
2. Open your account and the Preferences tab, at <https://cloud.layer5.io/account/preferences>.

How the controls behave:

- **Everything is on until you turn it off.** A new account receives every notification. You opt out of the ones you do not want, and a notification added later is on for you until you turn it off.
- **Preferences save themselves.** About one second after your last change, Layer5 Cloud saves it and confirms with "Notification preferences updated". There is no Save button.
- **Preferences are grouped.** The preferences appear under categories and sub-categories. Each category has a switch that turns every preference in it on or off at once. To opt out of all email, turn every category off.
- **A preference suppresses email, not the event.** The event still happens and still appears in the audit trail. Only the email is skipped.

The categories below are the ones the account page lists. Layer5 Cloud reads the list of available preferences from its own configuration, so a deployment can list more or fewer.

| Category | Preference | Emails you when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acknowledgment | Badge assignment and updates | A badge is awarded to you or changed. |
| Organization Activity | Organization update | An organization you belong to is updated. |
| Workspace Activity | Team, user, and organization management | A team you belong to is updated, or you are added to a team. |
| Workspace Activity | Role assignment and updates | Your roles change. |
| Workspace Activity | Comments on your designs | Someone comments on a design you own. Turning this off silences email about comments on your designs. |
| Workspace Activity | Participating and @mentions in comments | You are mentioned in a comment, or a thread you took part in gets a reply. |

To stop email from one thread without turning the preference off, mute that thread. See [Muting comment notifications]({{< ref "kanvas/designer/comments/index.md#muting-comment-notifications" >}}).

## Preferences that do nothing yet

Three preferences appear greyed out and unchecked, and cannot be changed: **Changes to designs**, **Deployments in environments**, and **Weekly summary**. Layer5 Cloud does not send those emails today. Do not rely on them.

There is no separate Approval Requests category, and there is no single switch that opts out of every email at once. Turn each category off to stop all email.

## Edge cases

- Anonymous accounts never receive organization update email.
- Layer5 Cloud checks the preference when it is about to send the email. Turning a preference back on does not resend email that was skipped while it was off.
- If saving fails, the page shows the reason, and your previous setting stays in force.

Who receives comment email is described in [Managing comment notifications]({{< ref "kanvas/designer/comments/index.md#managing-comment-notifications" >}}). Profile and sign-in settings are on [Setting up a Layer5 account]({{< ref "cloud/getting-started/getting-started-with-layer5-account.md" >}}).

## Hotfix - custom-domain orgs with anchored-fallback credentials hit 1722 at callback

Custom-domain orgs without their own BYOC IdP credentials (e.g. `exoscale.layer5.io`) ran into `meshery-cloud-1722 \state validation failed\` immediately after GitHub redirected back to `/oidc/callback/github`. The W2 state binding stamped the request host (`exoscale.layer5.io`), but the callback legitimately lands at the canonical host (`cloud.layer5.io`) because the fallback chain anchors `redirect_uri` there. The validator's strict host-binding equality refused the cross-host bounce.

### What changed

`OIDCStart` now stamps the **effective callback host** into the state payload, mirroring `composeCallbackURL`'s precedence:

- BYOC (`cred.CallbackHost` empty) -> stamp `req.Host`
- Anchored fallback (`cred.CallbackHost` set) -> stamp `cred.CallbackHost`

So the state's host-binding holds whether the callback lands on the same custom domain or on the canonical Provider Org host. `TestOIDCStart_ScenarioA2_CustomEtldFallback` now asserts `ValidateState(state, cookie,

## Hotfix - production sign-in restored on cloud.layer5.io (v1.0.97 regression)

Fixes a regression introduced in v1.0.97 where sign-in via GitHub / Google on `cloud.layer5.io` failed with `meshery-cloud-1729` \direct OIDC sign-in without a Hydra login_challenge is not yet supported\ (Cloudflare shows this as 502 from some POPs). The legacy Kratos selfservice OIDC flow initiated the Hydra login challenge internally; W2's `/oidc/start` had no equivalent, so the React `/login` page's \Sign in with...\ button forwarded to W2 without a `login_challenge` and OIDCCallback fell into its fail-closed branch.

### What changed

- `OIDCStart` now bounces server-side through Hydra's `/oauth2/auth` endpoint when the inbound URL lacks `?login_challenge=`, parses the freshly minted challenge out of the 302 `Location` header, and feeds it into the W2 state binding. The callback then has a valid challenge for `accept_login`, Hydra returns a code-carrying redirect to `/oauth/callback`, and `HandleRedirect` closes the loop via its existing code exchange + cookie issuance.
- The off-eTLD guard moved ahead of the new bounce so off-eTLD-custom-domain misconfigs surface the correct `meshery-cloud-1725` error instead of being masked by a bounce failure.

PR: #5392

## Hotfix - production sign-in restored on cloud.layer5.io

Fixes a regression where clicking **Sign in with GitHub** / **Sign in with Google** on `cloud.layer5.io/login` redirected users to the upstream OAuth provider with a `redirect_uri` of `https://cloud.layer5.io/kratos/self-service/methods/oidc/callback/{provider}`, which GitHub / Google rejected as edirect_uri is not associated with this application\ after the production OAuth App callback URL was updated to the W2 native path `/oidc/callback/{provider}`.

### What changed

- `OrgAuthData` exposes a new `UseCloudNativeOidc` boolean that is true for both registered custom-domain hosts AND for the canonical Provider Org host (`SERVER_BASE_URL`'s host). The React login / registration pages now gate the W2 cloud-native redirect on this field, so canonical-host sign-in no longer falls through to the legacy Kratos OIDC flow.
- A new `resolveOIDCOrgID(req)` helper in the server handlers prefers the middleware-resolved org and falls back to `ProviderOrgID` when the request lands on the canonical host. Both `OIDCStart` and `OIDCCallback` consume the helper so the state binding's `orgId` is symmetric across the round trip on the canonical host.

### Rollout notes

The Layer5 production GitHub OAuth App's Authorization callback URL is already `https://cloud.layer5.io/oidc/callback/github` and this deploy restores canonical-host sign-in without further OAuth App changes.

The staging GitHub OAuth App (1065875) must mirror this with `https://staging-cloud.layer5.io/oidc/callback/github` for staging sign-in to work after this deploys to staging. If that has not yet been updated, staging will exhibit the same symptom until it is.

PR: #5390

title: "Default Permissions"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/reference/default-permissions/index.md
description: List of default permissions granted to the Organizations, Teams and Users roles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

{{< alert title="Customizable Permissions" type="info" >}}Only a Provider Admin can create or change [keychains]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keychains.md" >}}) and [roles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/roles/_index.md" >}}). On hosted Layer5 Cloud, Layer5 operates the Provider Admin role, so an organization cannot build a custom permission set itself. On a self-hosted deployment, the operator's Provider Admins can. Changing the keychains of a role changes that role for every organization that uses it.{{< /alert >}}

**Legend:**

- ✅* user must be resource owner in order to perform action.
- ✅ user is allowed to perform action regardless of resource ownership.

<div class="permissions-tabpane">
{{< tabpane text=true >}}
{{< tab header="**Sort by**:" disabled=true />}}
{{< tab header="Categories" lang="en" >}}
{{< csvtable >}}
{{< /tab >}}
{{< tab header="Roles" lang="en" >}}

{{< /tabpane >}}

## How permission checks work

A permission is a named key that allows one action, such as Create Team. A keychain groups keys, and a role groups keychains. Layer5 Cloud checks the key, never the role name. Before it runs a guarded action, Cloud resolves the organization the request names, then checks whether the user holds the key through a role in that organization. A user's permissions are the union of the keys from every role the user holds there.

When a user lacks the key, Cloud refuses the request with HTTP 403 and the message "You do not hold the permission this action requires in this organization". The response body is JSON with an `error` message and a `code`.

Provider Admin passes every permission check, in every organization.

Keys, keychains, and roles are defined once for the whole deployment. What varies per organization is which roles a user holds there. See [Keys]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keys.md" >}}) and [Keychains]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keychains.md" >}}).

## Default roles

| Role | Scope | Assigned by |
|---|---|---|
| Provider Admin | Provider | Provider Admin |
| Kanvas | Provider | Provider Admin. Every new account receives it automatically. |
| Curator | Provider | Provider Admin |
| Organization Admin | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| User | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| Workspace Admin | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| Workspace Manager | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| Academy Admin | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| Academy Learner | Organization | Organization Admin or Provider Admin |
| Team Admin | Team | Team Admin or Provider Admin |

An anonymous user, someone using Kanvas without signing in, receives an internal Anonymous User role. It is not listed and cannot be assigned. See [Kanvas reference]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/_index.md" >}}) for what anonymous users can do in Kanvas.

The Kanvas role holds no keychains. It makes the Kanvas extension available when a Meshery Server connects to Layer5 Cloud.

## Roles the matrix columns do not cover

The tables above are refreshed from the Layer5 permission list (`static/data/csv/keys.csv`). A check mark means the role holds the permission. A check mark with an asterisk means the role holds the permission only on resources the user owns. A cross means the role does not hold the permission.

The spreadsheet includes columns for User, Team Admin, Academy Admin, Learner (headed Leaner), Workspace Admin, Org Billing Manager, Org Admin, and Provider Admin. These roles have no column:

| Role | What it holds by default |
|---|---|
| Workspace Manager | The permissions of Workspace Admin for workspaces, environments, teams, and lifecycle actions, plus management of the designs, environments, and connections inside the workspaces where the user holds the role. It does not hold the catalog curation permissions. |
| Curator | No keychains in a default install. Organization Admin and Workspace Admin hold the catalog curation permissions, including approving and denying publish requests. |
| Kanvas | No keychains. See [Default roles](#default-roles). |
| Anonymous User | The Kanvas design permissions for people who are not signed in. |

Academy Admin holds the Academy management permissions, plus team management and workspace management. Academy Learner holds access to Academy content and registration. Both appear as columns in the tables above.

## Default keychains

Layer5 Cloud ships 30 default keychains. Each groups the permissions for one area. Roles hold keychains, so granting a keychain to a role grants every permission in it. The system account owns the default keychains. Only a Provider Admin can change a keychain or assign one to a role, as of Layer5 Cloud v1.0.280.

| Keychain | What it groups |
|---|---|
| User View | Permissions for individual users, including View Tokens, View Sessions, View Keys, and View Keychains. |
| User Management | Managing users and their roles. |
| Team View | Viewing teams and their members. |
| Team Management | Managing teams and team membership. |
| Organization Management | Managing organizations, their teams, and their users. |
| Events Management | Event management: statistics, audit, and summaries. |
| Security Management | Creating, downloading, and deleting API tokens, and managing credentials. Key and keychain management belongs to Provider Management. See [security permission keys]({{< ref "cloud/reference/_index.md#permission-keys" >}}). |

Layer5 Cloud also ships keychains for workspaces, environments, the catalog, lifecycle actions, extensions, settings, performance, views, collaboration, infrastructure, curation, the Academy, and the two Kanvas action sets (Designer Actions and Operator Actions). For keychain behavior, see [Keychains]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keychains.md" >}}).

## Profile permissions

The profile permissions are not yet rows in the permission list. They are held by default as follows:

| Permission | Held by |
| --- | --- |
| View Profiles | User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin |
| Create Profile, Edit Profile, Delete Profile | Workspace Admin, Organization Admin |
| Assign profile to workspace, Remove profile from workspace | Workspace Admin, Academy Admin, Organization Admin |

Provider Admin holds all six. The owner of a profile can read it without View Profiles, and can edit it and its connection links without Edit Profile. People using Kanvas without signing in hold none of them. See [Profiles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/spaces/profiles.md" >}}).

## What the matrix does not show

- **Security keys.** Token, session, key, and keychain keys are not all rows in this spreadsheet. See [security permission keys]({{< ref "cloud/reference/_index.md#permission-keys" >}}).
- **Canvas editing.** The permission list omits the per-edit Kanvas permissions, such as adding, deleting, and styling components. See [Kanvas reference]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/_index.md" >}}) for which Kanvas actions check a permission.
- **Provider Admin.** It holds every permission, including permissions that are not in the list.
- **Plan limits.** A role grants a permission, and the plan decides whether the capability exists for the organization. See [Feature availability by plan]({{< ref "cloud/reference/_index.md#feature-availability-by-plan" >}}).

## Custom roles

A custom role bundles keychains that the default roles do not combine. Only a Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete a custom role, or change an existing role. The server refuses everyone else with HTTP 403. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, Layer5 operates the Provider Admin role, so an organization cannot create custom roles itself. On a self-hosted deployment, the operator's Provider Admins can.

Roles and keychains are defined for the whole Layer5 Cloud deployment, not per organization. Only a Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete a keychain, change its keys, or assign a keychain to a role. Changing the keychains of a role changes that role for every organization that uses it. See [Roles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/roles/_index.md" >}}).

The plan catalog lists Custom Roles and User-defined Roles as packaged capabilities. Layer5 Cloud does not check your plan when a custom role is created. It checks that the caller is a Provider Admin.

title: "Email / SMTP Troubleshooting"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/guides/self-hosted/operating/smtp/index.md
description: This guide explains how to diagnose email sending issues in Layer5 Cloud deployments using the enhanced debug logging and testing features.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Email Debugging Guide for Layer5 Cloud

This guide explains how to diagnose email sending issues in Layer5 Cloud deployments using the enhanced debug logging and testing features.

## Overview

Email issues in Layer5 Cloud can occur due to various reasons including SMTP configuration problems, template errors, recipient validation issues, or network connectivity problems. This guide provides comprehensive debugging tools and techniques.

{{< alert title="Read this before upgrading to v1.0.253 or later" type="warning" >}}
The shared mail server your deployment configures with `SMTP_HOST` and
`SMTP_PORT` is now screened the same way an Organization's own mail server is,
and **the server refuses to start when it fails that screen**. If `SMTP_HOST`
points at an in-cluster relay, at a non-submission port such as mailpit on
`1025`, or at a plaintext MTA, this deployment stops sending mail on upgrade
and says so at startup. See
[Constraints on the shared mail server](#constraints-on-the-shared-mail-server).
{{< /alert >}}

## Debug Log Levels

To enable email debugging, set `env.loglevel` in your Helm values to `5` (debug) or `6` (trace) and upgrade. The chart default is `4` (info). Return it to `4` when you finish, because debug logs record more detail.

```yaml
env:
  loglevel: 5
```

## Testing Email Configuration

### 1. Email Configuration Test Endpoint (Provider Admin Only) {#1-email-configuration-test-endpoint}

Check that the four `SMTP_*` values are configured, without sending an email.
**Both verbs of this endpoint require authentication and the provider admin
role**, so the `GET` must carry a credential. It validates configuration only -
it does not dial the SMTP server.

```bash
curl -X GET "https://your-domain.com/api/system/email/test" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT_TOKEN"
```

**Expected Response (Success):**

```json
{
  "status": "success",
  "message": "Email configuration is valid",
  "timestamp": "1695312000"
}
```

The response carries the verdict only. It does not report `smtp_host`,
`smtp_port` or `smtp_username`: those are the deployment's own relay settings,
and `SMTP_USERNAME` is an email address. Read the configured values from your
deployment configuration instead.

**Expected Response (Error):** `500 Internal Server Error`, as plain text
rather than JSON. The body is the error's short description alone - the full
error, which names the relay, stays in the log:

```text
SMTP configuration error for field 'SMTP_HOST'
```

**Expected Response (Unauthenticated):** `401 Unauthorized`

```json
{
  "message": "user must be logged in to perform this operation"
}
```

**Expected Response (Authenticated, not a provider admin):** `403 Forbidden`

```json
{
  "message": "user you@example.com must be Provider Admin to perform this operation"
}
```

### 2. Authenticated Email Send Test (Provider Admin Only)

Send an actual test email to verify end-to-end email functionality. This endpoint requires authentication and provider admin role:

```bash
curl -X POST "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/system/email/test" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT_TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "to": "test@example.com",
    "subject": "Layer5 Cloud Email Test"
  }'
```

**Request Body:**

```json
{
  "to": "test@example.com",
  "subject": "Layer5 Cloud Email Test (optional)"
}
```

**Expected Response (Success):**

```json
{
  "status": "success",
  "message": "Test email sent successfully",
  "timestamp": "1695312000",
  "sentTo": "test@example.com"
}
```

**Expected Response (Unauthenticated / not a provider admin):** the same `401`
and `403` JSON bodies as the `GET` above - both verbs carry the same
provider-admin gate.

**Expected Response (Error - Invalid Email):** `400 Bad Request`, as plain text:

```text
Invalid email address format
```

**Expected Response (Error - Email Configuration):** `500 Internal Server
Error`, as plain text. The configuration is checked before anything is sent, so
this is the same verdict the `GET` gives:

```text
SMTP configuration error for field 'SMTP_HOST'
```

**Expected Response (Error - the send itself failed):** `500 Internal Server
Error`, as plain text, carrying the short description only. The relay's own
reply, the resolved endpoint and the SMTP username stay in the log:

```text
Failed to send email with subject 'Layer5 Cloud Email Test' to recipients: test@example.com
```

### 3. Required Environment Variables

Either set all four values or leave all four empty. A deployment that leaves
them empty is a supported state - it simply sends no mail - but a deployment
that sets some of them and not others does not start.

| Variable | Chart value | Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SMTP_HOST` | `smtp.smtphost` | Must resolve to a publicly routable address |
| `SMTP_PORT` | `smtp.smtpport` | One of `25`, `465`, `587`, `2525` |
| `SMTP_USERNAME` | `smtp.smtpusername` | A full address: it becomes the `From` header |
| `SMTP_PASSWORD` | `smtp.smtppassword` | The mailbox password or app password |

`SMTP_PORT` also decides how the session is encrypted, because the four keys
carry no mode of their own: **`465` means implicit TLS**, and every other
permitted port takes STARTTLS. Read
[Constraints on the shared mail server](#constraints-on-the-shared-mail-server)
before you change either value.

## Constraints on the Shared Mail Server

Since **v1.0.253**, mail is routed per Organization: an Organization that has
[brought its own mail server]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/org-management/bring-your-own-mail-server.md" >}})
sends through that server, and everyone else sends through the shared mail
server your deployment configures. Both now go through **one** send primitive,
so the shared mail server is screened exactly as a tenant's is.

That screening is new. The previous send path applied none of it, so a
deployment that has been sending mail happily can be refused after an upgrade.
A self-hosted install that points `SMTP_HOST` at an internal, plaintext, or non-submission relay can be refused.

### What is refused

| Constraint | What is refused | How to fix it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Submission port allowlist** | any port other than `25`, `465`, `587` or `2525` - for example mailpit on `1025` | move the relay onto a submission port, or put a submission-port listener in front of it |
| **Internal-address screen** | an `SMTP_HOST` that resolves to loopback, RFC 1918 private, IPv6 unique-local, RFC 6598 carrier-shared or link-local space - for example an in-cluster `mailhog.default.svc` | point `SMTP_HOST` at a publicly routable relay. There is deliberately no allowlist or opt-out setting |
| **STARTTLS is required** | a relay that answers but does not advertise the extension - a plaintext internal MTA | enable STARTTLS on the relay. It is refused rather than downgraded, because a downgrade would put the mailbox password on the wire in the clear |
| **`SMTP_PORT` parses as a number** | a stray character or space in the value, such as `"587 "` | correct the value in your Secret or environment file |
| **`SMTP_USERNAME` parses as an RFC 5322 address** | a bare mailbox name such as `no-reply` with no domain - it becomes the `From:` header | use the full mailbox address |

**Every address `SMTP_HOST` resolves to is screened, not just the one a
connection happens to use.** A host publishing both a public and a private
record is refused.

Port `465` is the exception to STARTTLS: it speaks TLS from the first byte, and
the deployment selects that mode automatically from the port. You do not
configure the encryption mode separately.

### What happens at startup

The server validates the shared mail server once, at startup, rather than
waiting for somebody's password reset to fail silently. Only the first row below
stops the deployment:

| At startup | Verdict | What you see |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The configuration fails one of the constraints above | **the server exits** | `meshery_cloud-3301` at Error, then exit code 1 |
| The relay could not be reached at all - DNS did not answer, or the connection did not complete | the server starts | `meshery_cloud-3302` at Error |
| The relay answered but its certificate did not verify - expired, wrong host name, or an untrusted issuer | the server starts | `meshery_cloud-3304` at Error, naming the relay host |
| None of the four `SMTP_*` values is set | the server starts | a warning naming the first unset key |
| The relay answered and the screens passed | the server starts | `INFO The shared mail relay answered on smtp.example.com:587 over starttls` |

The two non-fatal failures are still failures: **no mail leaves over the shared
mail server until they clear.** Treat `3302` and `3304` at startup as a page,
not a note. They are separate codes because the remedy is different - `3302` is
the network, `3304` is the relay's certificate.

A refusal is fatal on purpose. The alternative is a deployment that comes up
green and drops every message silently, which is the failure this check exists
to convert into a refusal to start.

The startup check **does not authenticate and sends no message**. A rotated
password is not a reason a deployment will not start, and an authentication
failure is not one of the verdicts this check acts on.

{{< alert title="The configuration test endpoint does not dial" type="info" >}}
`GET /api/system/email/test` now applies everything above that can be decided
without a connection - the presence of all four keys, the port allowlist, the
shape of the host, and the two parse rules. It still opens no connection, so
whether the relay offers STARTTLS is the startup check's answer to give, not
this endpoint's.
{{< /alert >}}

## Debug Log Examples

When `env.loglevel` is `5`, you'll see detailed debug logs for email operations.

{{< alert title="The transport is no longer described in the send logs" type="info" >}}
The lines that echoed the relay host, port and SMTP username before every send
were removed in **v1.0.253**.
The transport is now chosen in one place for both senders, so it is reported
once at startup instead of being restated by every message - and `SMTP_USERNAME`
is an email address, which does not belong in a line emitted per send. If you
are grepping for `SMTP Configuration Debug`, `Attempting SMTP send`,
`Email construction completed`, `SMTP send failed - detailed error info`, or
any of the `Flow email` lines that named a host, they no longer exist.
{{< /alert >}}

### 1. The Shared Mail Server, at Startup {#1-smtp-configuration-validation}

This is where the relay is described now, once per process:

```log
INFO The shared mail relay answered on smtp.example.com:587 over starttls
```

When none of the four values is set, the deployment starts and says so:

```log
WARN The shared mail relay is not configured (SMTP_HOST is unset). No transactional or identity mail can be sent over it; organizations with their own mail server are unaffected
```

A refusal names the constraint that refused it and the process exits; see
[What happens at startup](#what-happens-at-startup).

### 2. Template Processing

```log
DEBUG Email template parsing template_paths=[email-templates/meshery-cloud/email.body.gotmpl, ...] template_count=5 base_template_path=email-templates/meshery-cloud/email.body.gotmpl
DEBUG Email template parsed template_name=email.body.gotmpl
DEBUG Executing email template email_type=welcome recipients=user@example.com has_org_vars=true org_name=MyOrg
DEBUG Email template executed body_length=2048 email_type=welcome
```

### 3. Sending {#3-email-construction-and-sending}

```log
DEBUG Email sending attempt initiated subject="Welcome to Layer5 Cloud" recipient_count=1 cc_count=0
INFO Email sent recipients=user@example.com subject="Welcome to Layer5 Cloud"
```

### 4. Error Scenarios

A failed send is logged as its structured error, carrying a code:

```log
ERROR meshery_cloud-1145: SMTP send mail error
```

For a message that belonged to an Organization with its own mail server, the
failure is recorded against that Organization as well - see
[Which mail server a message left through](#which-mail-server-a-message-left-through).

## Flow Emails (Kratos Integration)

Identity mail reaches Layer5 Cloud only when Kratos uses the HTTP courier, which posts each message to `/api/identity/flow/emails`. Layer5 Cloud then renders it with the signup organization's branding and sends it like other application mail. Under the HTTP courier there is no SMTP fallback. When Layer5 Cloud answers anything but a success, Kratos retries the message (five times by default) and then abandons it, with no visible error to the user. With the default SMTP courier, Kratos sends the mail itself through `kratos.kratos.config.courier.smtp.connection_uri`, and the shared-relay rules on this page do not apply to it.

Flow emails that do arrive are rendered by the same process and logged through the same
structured logger. They used to be written to standard output with a `[DEBUG]`
prefix, echoing the relay host and the SMTP username past the logger at a level
nothing could turn down; those lines no longer exist.

**Only two Kratos template types are dispatched:** `verification_code_valid`
and `recovery_code_valid`. Every environment runs the `code` strategy for
recovery and verification, so those are the only two Kratos emits - and the
unknown-recipient notices (`recovery_code_invalid`, `verification_code_invalid`)
are deliberately not sent. Any other type is acknowledged with a `200` and
logged as unsupported rather than mailed; a `200` for one of those means the
request was accepted and no message was sent.

```log
DEBUG Flow email attempt.  subject_template:  email-templates/valid/email-recover-subject.body.gotmpl , body_template:  email-templates/valid/email-recover.body.gotmpl , organization_id:  0e6b7ba0-... , recipient:  user@example.com
DEBUG Flow email delivery failed.  error_type:  *errors.Error , template_type:  recovery_code_valid , organization_id:  0e6b7ba0-... , recipient:  user@example.com
INFO Flow email sent.  template_type:  recovery_code_valid , recipient:  user@example.com
```

## Which Mail Server a Message Left Through

Every message this deployment sends is routed by the reader's Organization. An
Organization that has configured its own mail server, verified its from domain
and turned it on sends through that server; every other message takes the shared
mail server configured by `SMTP_HOST`.

That routing produces its own log lines, and a self-hosted operator will meet
them without having configured anything themselves:

- **The Organization's mail server was used and the message was accepted.** No
  operator action; the verdict is recorded against that Organization's delivery
  health, which its administrators read on the Email tab.

- **The Organization's mail server refused the message and fallback is on.** The
  message is re-sent over the shared mail server, arriving from this
  deployment's address with the Organization's name and a `(via ...)` suffix.
  Logged as `meshery_cloud-3299`.

- **The Organization's mail server refused the message and fallback is off.**
  The message is **dropped**, logged as `meshery_cloud-3300` at Critical. This
  is that Organization's own setting working as documented, not a fault in this
  deployment - but a dropped verification or recovery message locks a user out
  of their account, so it is worth alerting on.

- **The Organization's mail server took the whole message and never answered.**
  Delivery is unknown, so the message is deliberately **not** re-sent over the
  shared mail server - re-sending it could deliver it twice. Logged as
  `meshery_cloud-3303` at Critical.

- **The Organization's stored configuration could not be read** - a database
  read failed, or a stored password would not decrypt, usually after
  `CLOUD_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` was rotated. The message takes the shared
  mail server whatever that Organization's fallback setting says, because the
  fault is this deployment's rather than a delivery policy the tenant chose.
  Logged as `meshery_cloud-3298`.

The full behavior an Organization administrator sees is documented in
[Bring Your Own Mail Server]({{< ref "cloud/guides/organizations/org-management/bring-your-own-mail-server.md" >}}).

## Common Issues and Solutions

### 1. SMTP Configuration Errors

**Issue:** `SMTP configuration error: SMTP_HOST is empty`

**Solution:**

- Verify all SMTP environment variables are set
- Check that environment variables are properly loaded in your deployment
- Use the test endpoint to validate configuration

### 2. Authentication Failures

**Issue:** `SMTP authentication was refused by the mail server`

**Solution:**

- Verify SMTP username and password are correct
- For Gmail, use App Passwords instead of regular passwords
- Check if 2FA is enabled and properly configured

The identity that was refused and the endpoint it was presented to are in the
log's long description (`authenticating as <username> at <host:port>`), never in
the response - an SMTP username is an email address.

### 3. Template Errors

**Issue:** `Email template missing or inaccessible`

**Solution:** the templates ship inside the Layer5 Cloud image. If you built a custom image or mounted a volume over its configuration directory, restore the bundled templates, and confirm that the image tag matches the release you run.

### 4. Recipient Validation Errors

**Issue:** `Email recipient validation failed`

**Solution:**

- Verify email addresses are valid and properly formatted
- Check for empty recipient lists
- Validate email addresses contain `@` symbol
- Check for a carriage return or line feed in an address. An address carrying
  one is **refused**, not sanitized: recipient addresses are written as SMTP
  protocol verbs and into the header block, so a line break in one would start a
  header of its own. This applies to `Cc` addresses as well as `To`

Subjects are the deliberate asymmetry: a line break in a subject is stripped
rather than refused, because a subject is display text and dropping a
notification over a design name containing a newline would turn a cosmetic
problem into a lost message.

### 5. Network Connectivity Issues

**Issue:** `meshery_cloud-3302` at startup, or `dial tcp: lookup smtp.example.com: no such host`

**Solution:**

- Check network connectivity to SMTP server
- Verify egress from this cluster to the relay's submission port is allowed
- Test DNS resolution for SMTP host

No mail leaves over the shared mail server while this is outstanding, even
though the deployment started.

### 6. The Server Will Not Start After an Upgrade

**Issue:** `meshery_cloud-3301` at Error, then exit code 1.

**Solution:** the shared mail server fails one of the
[constraints](#what-is-refused). The logged cause names which screen refused it:

| Cause code | The screen that refused | What to change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| meshery_cloud-3297 | a key is unset, `SMTP_PORT` is not a number, or `SMTP_USERNAME` is not an RFC 5322 address | correct the named key |
| meshery_cloud-3262 | the host is empty, or carries whitespace or a line break | correct `SMTP_HOST` |
| meshery_cloud-3263 | the port is not a submission port, or the host resolved into internal address space | correct `SMTP_PORT`, or point `SMTP_HOST` at a publicly routable relay |
| meshery_cloud-3265 | the relay answered and does not offer STARTTLS. Only reachable on a port other than `465`, which never negotiates STARTTLS | enable STARTTLS on the relay, or move it to `465` for implicit TLS |

### 7. The Server's Certificate Is Not Trusted

**Issue:** `meshery_cloud-3304` at Error; the deployment starts.

**Solution:** the relay answered, and its certificate did not verify against the
trusted roots - it has expired, was issued for a different host name, or is
self-signed or from an issuer this server does not trust. Fix the certificate;
this is not a network fault and not something egress rules will clear. Every
send fails identically until it verifies.

## Development Mode

In development environment (`ENVIRONMENT=development`), the rendered email
content is logged **in addition to** being sent, so the body can be read without
opening the recipient's mailbox:

```log
INFO Development mode - Email details recipients=user@example.com subject="Test Email" body="<html>...</html>"
```

The message still goes out over the shared mail server, which still has to
satisfy the [constraints](#what-is-refused) above. Pointing a development
deployment at a local catch-all mailbox on port `1025` does not work.

## Error Codes Reference

| Error Code | Description | Common Causes |
|------------|-------------|---------------|
| meshery_cloud-1092 | Failed to send email | Network issues, SMTP server down |
| meshery_cloud-1144 | SMTP authentication was refused by the mail server | Invalid credentials. The refused identity and the endpoint reach the log only |
| meshery_cloud-1145 | SMTP send mail error | Server rejection, quota exceeded |
| meshery_cloud-1146 | SMTP configuration error | Missing environment variables |
| meshery_cloud-1147 | Email template missing | Template files not found |
| meshery_cloud-1148 | Email recipient validation failed | Invalid email addresses, an empty recipient list, or an address containing a carriage return or line feed |

### Mail routing and the shared mail server

These codes arrived with per-Organization mail routing in **v1.0.253**.
The four marked **send path** describe a message that belonged to an
Organization with its own mail server; the rest describe the shared mail server
this deployment configures.

| Error Code | At startup | Meaning |
|------------|------------|---------|
| meshery_cloud-3297 | cause of 3301 | The shared mail server is not usable as configured: a key is unset, `SMTP_PORT` is not a port number, or `SMTP_USERNAME` is not an address. The log names the key, never its value. The same faults are reported under this code by `/api/system/email/test` and by a send |
| meshery_cloud-3298 | send path | An Organization's mail server configuration could not be read, so the message went over the shared mail server |
| meshery_cloud-3299 | send path | A delivery over an Organization's own mail server failed. The endpoint is in the log only |
| meshery_cloud-3300 | send path | Nothing was sent: an Organization's mail server refused the message and its fallback is turned off |
| meshery_cloud-3301 | **exits** | The shared mail server fails one of the [constraints](#what-is-refused) - port, address, or no STARTTLS. The cause names which screen refused it |
| meshery_cloud-3302 | starts | DNS or the connection did not complete. Genuine unreachability only; no mail leaves over the shared mail server until it clears |
| meshery_cloud-3303 | send path | An Organization's mail server took the whole message and never acknowledged it. Recorded as uncertain and **not** re-sent, because re-sending could deliver it twice |
| meshery_cloud-3304 | starts | The shared mail server's certificate failed verification - expiry, host name or issuer. Check the certificate, not the network |

## Monitoring and Alerting

Consider setting up monitoring for email-related metrics:

1. **Email Send Success Rate**: Monitor successful vs failed email sends
2. **SMTP Response Times**: Track SMTP server response times
3. **Template Processing Time**: Monitor email template rendering performance
4. **Configuration Validation**: Regular health checks for email configuration

## Best Practices

1. **Use Debug Logs Sparingly**: Only enable debug logging when troubleshooting
2. **Secure Credentials**: Never log SMTP passwords in plaintext
3. **Regular Testing**: Use the test endpoint to validate configuration regularly
4. **Monitor Quotas**: Keep track of email service provider quotas and limits
5. **Template Validation**: Test email templates thoroughly before deployment

## Troubleshooting Checklist

- [ ] Set `env.loglevel` to `5` for debug logging while you diagnose
- [ ] Verify all SMTP environment variables are configured
- [ ] Confirm `SMTP_PORT` is one of `25`, `465`, `587`, `2525`, and that `SMTP_USERNAME` is a full address
- [ ] Confirm `SMTP_HOST` resolves only to publicly routable addresses, and that the relay offers STARTTLS (or is on `465`)
- [ ] Read the startup log for `meshery_cloud-3301`, `-3302` or `-3304` before looking anywhere else
- [ ] Test email configuration using the provider-admin-only `/api/system/email/test` endpoint, authenticating the request
- [ ] Check network connectivity to SMTP server
- [ ] Validate email template files exist and are accessible
- [ ] Verify recipient email addresses are valid
- [ ] Check SMTP server logs for additional error details
- [ ] Monitor email service provider quotas and limits


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Environments"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/concepts/spaces/environments/index.md
description: Environments are how you organize your deployment targets (whether on-premises servers or cloud services) into resource groups.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

An environment is a named group of connections, such as Kubernetes clusters, together with the credentials those connections use. Environments matter for two reasons:

- **An environment is a deploy target.** When you deploy a design, you choose the environment to deploy it to, and the design deploys to that environment's connections.
- **An environment is how a workspace exposes connections.** A workspace never holds connections directly. It holds environments, and teams assigned to the workspace reach the connections inside them.

Group connections the way you deploy: one environment per pipeline stage, region, or purpose. An environment belongs to one organization for its whole life. Editing an environment never changes its organization. Every member of the organization can list and open every environment in it. Team membership does not narrow the list.

{{< alert type="info" title="Looking for Practical Environment Management?" >}}
For step-by-step instructions on how to view, create, and edit environments, and how to assign connections to an environment or remove them from it, see the [Managing Environments]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-environments/index.md" >}}) guide.
{{< /alert >}}

### Assigning Resources to Environments

Assign any number of Connections to an environment whether that Connection is managed or unmanaged (see [MeshSync](https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/architecture/meshsync) to learn more about managed and unmanaged Connections). In-turn, assign any number of Environments to one or more [Workspaces]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/spaces/workspaces.md" >}}). Connections (and any associated Credentials) that are assigned to an Environment become immediately available for use in any associated Workspace.

### Sharing Resources between Environments

Environments can share resources. For example, you might create an environment named "production" and assign three connections: a GitHub connection, a Kubernetes connection, and a Prometheus connection. Subsequently, you also define an environment named "dev/test" and assign three connections: a different Kubernetes connection, a different Prometheus connection, _and_ the same GitHub connection that is also assigned to the "production" environment.

### Deleting an Environment

Deleting an environment does not delete any resources (e.g. connections) currently contained in the environment. Resources that belong to other environments will continue to belong to those other environments. Learn more about the behavior of [lifecycle of connections](https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/logical/connections). For the steps themselves, see [Delete an Environment]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-environments/index.md#delete-an-environment" >}}).

## Summary

Environments represent a collection of resources in the form of Connections - both of managed and unmanaged Connections. Environment resources are comprised of Connections (and implicitly any Credentials used by those assigned Connections). Create and use environments to organize your connections and credentials into groups, and then make these resources available to you and your teams by assigning environments to Workspaces.

## Key Features

- **Logical Grouping** Environments allow you to logically group related connections and their associated credentials. This makes it easier to manage, share, and work with a subset of resources instead of dealing with all your connections individually.

- **Resource Sharing** Environments can be seamlessly assigned to [Workspaces]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/spaces/workspaces.md" >}}), another essential concept in Meshery. When you assign an Environment to a Workspace, you enable resource sharing among team members. This collaborative approach simplifies the sharing of connections and resources, making it easier to work together in cloud native environments.

## Key Components

### Connections

Connections are an integral part of Environment. These are cloud native resources that can be both managed and unmanaged, and they're registered by the Meshery Server. Examples of connections include Kubernetes clusters, Prometheus instances, Jaeger tracers, and Nginx web servers.

> See "[Connections](https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/logical/connections)" in Meshery Docs for more information.

### Credentials

Credentials in an Environment are the keys to securely authenticate and access managed connections. For example, valid Prometheus secrets or Kubernetes API tokens are essential credentials for securely interacting with these managed resources.

> See "[Credentials](https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/logical/credentials)" in Meshery Docs for more information.

## Access Control for Connections and Credentials

Access to a Connection, and therefore to its associated Credentials, is granted through any one of the following, evaluated independently:

1. **Direct ownership**  -  the Connection's owner (User ID) matches the current user's ID. Ownership grants full read and write access, including deleting the Connection and its Credentials.
2. **Indirect access through a shared Workspace**  -  the Connection is assigned to an Environment linked to a Workspace, and the current user belongs to a Team with access to that Workspace. This grants **read-only** access; Team membership alone does not grant the right to modify or delete the Connection or its Credentials.
3. **The "View All Organizations" key**  -  a user holding this [key]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keys.md" >}}) can access every Connection and Credential across all organizations, bypassing the ownership and Team checks above.

> Designs and Views are governed by a separate mechanism  -  resource-access mappings  -  rather than inheriting through Workspace/Team membership. See [Identity and Security → Security Boundaries]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/_index.md#security-boundaries" >}}) for how these mechanisms fit together.

## Example: Orbital Labs Environment Setup

The following illustrates how Five and Zara set up multi-cloud environments at Orbital Labs, spanning AWS, GCP, and Azure. See [Meet Five and the Cast]({{< ref "cloud/getting-started/meet-five/_index.md" >}}) for the full seed inventory.

### Environment Inventory

| Environment | Workspace | Cloud Provider | Connections |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prod-aws` | orbital-production | AWS | EKS cluster, RDS (PostgreSQL), S3, CloudFront, SQS |
| `prod-gcp` | orbital-production | GCP | GKE cluster, Cloud SQL, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub |
| `staging-aws` | orbital-staging | AWS | EKS cluster, S3, ElastiCache |
| `staging-azure` | orbital-staging | Azure | AKS cluster, Azure Blob Storage, Azure Service Bus |
| `dev-local` | orbital-dev | Local | kind (local Kubernetes), LocalStack (AWS emulation) |
| `stellar-enterprise` | stellar-main | Azure | AKS, Azure SQL, Azure API Management, Azure AD |

### Connecting prod-aws

Five connects Orbital Labs' primary AWS production environment to Layer5 Cloud:

1. Navigate to **Environments** and click **Create** (see [Create an Environment]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-environments/index.md#create-an-environment" >}}))
2. Name it `prod-aws` and save
3. Add connections one at a time  -  each connection is a discrete cloud resource:
   - **EKS cluster**: the compute layer for deployed workloads
   - **RDS (PostgreSQL)**: the managed database instance
   - **S3 bucket**: object storage for design artifacts and state
   - **CloudFront distribution**: CDN layer for the frontend
   - **SQS queue**: async messaging between services
4. Zara assigns `prod-aws` to the `orbital-production` workspace, making all five connections available to Infrastructure team members

### Adding prod-gcp for Multi-Cloud Coverage

Five repeats the process for GCP to give Orbital Labs multi-cloud flexibility:

1. Create environment `prod-gcp`
2. Add connections:
   - **GKE cluster**: Google Kubernetes Engine compute
   - **Cloud SQL**: managed relational database on GCP
   - **Cloud Storage bucket**: GCP object storage
   - **Pub/Sub topic**: async messaging on GCP
3. Zara assigns `prod-gcp` to `orbital-production` alongside `prod-aws`

Both environments are now readable by teams assigned to the `orbital-production` workspace. Deploying a design still offers environments from the organization's whole list, so choose the target deliberately.

{{< alert type="info" title="dev-local for Getting Started" >}}
The `dev-local` environment uses a local Kubernetes cluster (kind) and LocalStack to emulate AWS services, with no cloud credentials required. If you are following along with these docs for the first time, start with `dev-local` in the `orbital-dev` workspace.
{{< /alert >}}

## Choosing an environment at deploy time

Deploying a design happens in Kanvas. The deploy action offers environments from your organization's whole list at the moment you deploy. The workspace the design sits in does not limit that choice, so a design in a staging workspace can still be deployed to a production environment. Choose the target deliberately. See [Deploying Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/tasks/designs/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}).

## Platform-provisioned environments

Some environments are created by Layer5 Cloud itself to hold organization configuration, such as sign-in providers or the mail server. They appear in your organization's environment list, but they are not deploy targets you manage:

- They cannot be deleted. The attempt is refused with `this environment is provisioned by the platform and cannot be deleted here`.
- Connections cannot be assigned to them or detached from them through the normal environment controls.
- They cannot be added to a workspace. If one is already in a workspace, you can remove it.

Every environment you create is an ordinary environment.

## Limits and behavior

- Names and descriptions are limited to 255 characters. Names are not unique: two environments in one organization can share a name.
- **Editing replaces both fields.** An environment edit sets both the name and the description. A field left out of the request becomes empty, so always send both.
- **Organization is fixed.** An edit never moves an environment to another organization.
- A connection can be in any number of environments. Adding it to one does not remove it from another.
- An environment can be in any number of workspaces in its organization.
- **Removing a connection that was never assigned** is refused with `no such connection assignment`.
- Deleting an environment ends its connection assignments and its workspace assignments in one step. The connections remain, and keep their membership in any other environment.

## Permissions

Every environment action is checked in the organization that owns the environment. The keys are View Environment, Create Environment, Edit Environment, Delete Environment, Assign connections to environment, Remove connections from environment, Assign environment to workspace, and Remove environment from workspace. Default holders are in [Default Permissions]({{< ref "cloud/reference/default-permissions.md" >}}).

The feature matrix lists environments under the Enterprise plan. Layer5 Cloud does not refuse environment actions by plan: creating, editing, deleting, and assigning environments are governed only by the permissions above.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Profiles"
url: /pr-preview/pr-1353/cloud/concepts/spaces/profiles/index.md
description: A profile is a named record that represents one person or persona in an organization, groups the connections it publishes through, and is shared through workspaces.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A profile is a named record that belongs to one organization. It represents a person or a persona, such as the platform accounts someone publishes through, and it groups existing connections under that identity. Profiles are shared with people by assigning them to workspaces.

A profile is not your user account profile, and it is not a Meshery performance profile.

## What a profile holds

- a **name** (required, up to 255 characters, not unique) and an optional **description** (up to 1000 characters)
- an **owner**, who must be a signed-in member of the profile's organization
- optionally, the **user** the profile represents
- free-form **metadata**
- links to **connections**. A profile links to connections that already exist; it never copies them. Removing a link leaves the connection untouched.

A profile can be assigned to any number of workspaces in its own organization. Its organization is fixed for the life of the profile.

## Who can see a profile

A profile is visible to:

- its owner,
- the Organization Admins of its organization, and
- members of any team assigned to a workspace the profile is assigned to.

The owner always sees their own profile, whether or not it is in a workspace and even without the **View Profiles** permission. Organization Admins and workspace members also need **View Profiles**. Provider Admins do not see profiles automatically. Seeing a profile does not give you access to its linked connections, which keep their own access rules.

A profile that is in no workspace is visible only to its owner and the organization's admins. What you can change is never wider than what you can see: a profile you cannot see answers 404, the same as one that does not exist.

## Owner and succession

The owner can always edit their own profile and its connection links. Deleting a profile still needs the **Delete Profile** permission. Changing the owner transfers the profile.

When the owner's account is deleted, the profile passes to the earliest Organization Admin of its organization, or else to its earliest member, the same rule the organization follows for designs. A profile is never deleted because its owner's account was.

## Permissions

| Permission | Allows |
| --- | --- |
| View Profiles | Listing and reading the profiles you can see, and their connections. Owners read their own profiles without it. |
| Create Profile | Creating a profile in an organization |
| Edit Profile | Editing any visible profile, transferring its ownership, and linking or unlinking connections |
| Delete Profile | Deleting a profile |
| Assign profile to workspace | Assigning a visible profile to a workspace |
| Remove profile from workspace | Removing a profile from a workspace |

Every organization member holds **View Profiles**. Workspace Admins, Organization Admins and Provider Admins hold the rest, and Academy Admins can also assign profiles to workspaces and remove them. People using Kanvas without signing in hold none of them, and every profile change refuses a guest session. See [Default Permissions]({{< ref "cloud/reference/default-permissions.md#profile-permissions" >}}).

To create and share profiles, see [Managing Profiles]({{< ref "cloud/guides/workspaces/managing-profiles/index.md" >}}).

Contributing guides on documentation and video gallery
